Picture this: you're settled into your seat on a United flight out of LAX, the Pacific stretching endlessly outside your window, and you know — you genuinely know — that the person next to you paid $400 for this exact seat while you paid **7,500 miles**. That's the Hawaiian sweet spot, and it's one of the most quietly powerful redemptions available to anyone building a travel rewards strategy. Hawaii has always been the aspirational American vacation. It's the honeymoon destination, the bucket-list family trip, the anniversary getaway. And because of that demand, flights from the mainland — especially during spring break, summer, and the holidays — rarely go on sale. A round-trip economy ticket from Los Angeles to Honolulu will routinely run **$400–$700**, and during peak travel windows, prices can push past $1,000 for a family of four. That's real money. FI-community money. Now consider what Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles charges for that same seat: **7,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of cash pricing ($200 for a one-way), you're extracting **2.7 cents per point**. At the high end ($500 during peak season), that same 7,500 miles is worth **6.7 cents per point** — a figure that makes even seasoned travel rewards enthusiasts do a double-take. For context, most people in the points world consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. **Getting 6.7 cents per point is extraordinary.** It's not a fluke or a loophole — it's a structural pricing inefficiency baked into the Turkish award chart, which treats all short-haul domestic U.S. flights (including Hawaii, which is technically a domestic route) at the same rock-bottom rate. This is the fundamental insight behind every great travel rewards redemption: **loyalty programs price awards based on their own logic, not cash fares.** Turkish Miles & Smiles sees LAX→HNL as a short Star Alliance partner flight. The fact that cash fares on that route are elevated because of destination demand is irrelevant to their award chart. That gap — between what Turkish charges in miles and what the market charges in dollars — is exactly where you save. For a ChooseFI community member who already holds Citi ThankYou Points, this redemption is within reach right now. You don't need to fly Turkish. You don't need to connect through Istanbul. You just need availability on United, 7,500 miles, and about 20 minutes.

The magic here comes down to one core concept: Star Alliance partner pricing on a domestic U.S. route.

Turkish Airlines is a Star Alliance member, and like most alliance programs, they allow their members to book award flights on partner airlines — including United. Where Turkish gets interesting (and generous) is in how they price those partner awards. Their award chart uses a fixed, distance-based or zone-based structure, and for short-haul U.S. domestic flights, the price bottoms out at 7,500 miles one-way in economy.

Here's the pricing inefficiency in plain language: Turkish Miles & Smiles doesn't care that Hawaii is an aspirational, high-demand destination. To their award chart, LAX→HNL is just another short domestic United flight. Meanwhile, United's own MileagePlus program charges significantly more for the same route — often 13,000–22,500 miles one-way depending on the fare bucket. Turkish is pricing the same seat at less than half what United charges its own members. That's the gap you're exploiting.

No fuel surcharges — ever. This is a critical detail that makes Turkish a standout program. Many European programs (we're looking at you, Lufthansa Miles & More) pile on hundreds of dollars in fuel surcharges that nearly erase the value of the award. Turkish charges zero fuel surcharges on any award flight, including partner redemptions. Your out-of-pocket cost when booking this redemption is taxes and fees only — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary.

The most accessible path to 7,500 Turkish miles runs through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio. The transfer is instant — meaning you can see award availability, confirm your plan, and have the miles in your Turkish account within minutes, not days. That speed matters because Hawaii saver availability can disappear quickly.

You can also transfer from Bilt Rewards at 1:1 (also instant), or Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio (takes 1–5 days and is far less efficient — avoid Marriott for this transfer unless you have no other option).

The best Citi cards for earning ThankYou Points include the Citi Strata Premier, which earns 3x on dining, groceries, hotels, and airfare — categories that make accumulating 7,500 points genuinely fast for most households.

Turkish's award chart is fixed, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand, time of year, or how close you are to departure (beyond the booking window). A saver economy award on a short domestic U.S. United flight is always 7,500 miles. No dynamic pricing surprises. No "off-peak vs. peak" tiers to navigate. This predictability is itself a feature — you can plan around it.

The booking window opens 355 days in advance, giving you nearly a full year of search runway to find the availability you need.

Here's exactly how to execute this redemption from zero to booked.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm that saver economy availability exists on your target route and dates. Go to united.com, enter your origin and destination (for example, LAX to HNL), and select your travel dates. When the results appear, look specifically for fares labeled "Saver" — these are the award inventory buckets that partner programs like Turkish can access. Standard or Everyday awards will NOT be bookable through Turkish.

Search for "Saver" fares in economy and note the exact flight numbers, dates, and times. Take a screenshot — you'll need these details when you move to the Turkish website.

Tip: United's calendar view lets you scan a full month for saver availability. Use it. Flexibility of even 1–2 days can be the difference between finding a seat and hitting a wall.

Go to turkishairlines.com and navigate to the Miles & Smiles award booking tool. Search the same route and dates you identified on United. Turkish's search engine pulls real-time Star Alliance availability, so what you see here is what you can book. If the saver seats from Step 1 appear, you're ready to move.

Important: If you don't yet have a Turkish Miles & Smiles account, create one now — it's free and takes just a few minutes.

Once you've confirmed award availability, transfer your points. Log into your Citi ThankYou account (or Bilt Rewards account), navigate to the transfer partner section, and select Turkish Airlines Miles & Smiles. Enter the amount — 7,500 points per one-way flight — and confirm.

Citi and Bilt transfers to Turkish are instant. Your miles will appear in your Turkish account within minutes. Do not transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 2 — points transfers are one-way and non-refundable.

Return to the Turkish award booking tool with your miles now loaded. Complete the booking for your confirmed flight. You'll pay only taxes and fees at checkout — typically $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. itinerary. Enter your payment details for that small amount and complete the reservation.

You'll receive a booking confirmation from Turkish. The actual ticket is on United metal, so you'll also see the reservation appear in United's system using your confirmation code.

Hawaii saver availability on United can be tight, especially during peak travel periods. Here's your playbook:

Let's make this concrete. It's late February, and you're planning a spring getaway to Honolulu with your partner. You pull up United.com and search LAX→HNL for mid-April — not peak spring break week, but the week after, when families have gone home and the island is quieter. You find saver economy availability on a direct United flight departing at 8:45 AM and arriving in Honolulu before noon local time.

The cash price for that ticket: $389 per person one-way. For two travelers, that's $778 before you've booked the return.

The points price: 7,500 Turkish Miles & Smiles miles per person, plus roughly $11 in taxes and fees. For two people, you're spending 15,000 miles and about $22.

You already have 20,000 Citi ThankYou Points sitting in your account from everyday spending on your Citi Strata Premier — groceries, dining, a couple of utility bills. You transfer 15,000 points to Turkish Miles & Smiles (instant transfer), log into the Turkish booking portal, and complete both seats in a single transaction.

Your CPP on this redemption: $389 ÷ 7,500 = 5.2 cents per point. That's more than three times what most people consider a strong redemption.

Now for the experience itself: you're flying United Economy on a widebody aircraft — typically a Boeing 767 or 777 on the Honolulu route from LAX. The flight is approximately 5.5 hours. Economy isn't business class, but United's Pacific routes are comfortable — you'll find decent legroom in Economy Plus if you want to upgrade your seat selection for a modest fee, complimentary entertainment, and meal service on this longer domestic segment. The flight across the Pacific, even in economy, has a different feel than a 2-hour domestic hop. The water below you turns that impossible shade of blue. You land in Honolulu at mid-morning, cleared customs quickly (domestic flight — no customs required), and you're at your hotel before lunch.

Total cost for two one-way tickets: 15,000 miles + $22. Cash equivalent: $778. Money saved: $756. That's a car payment, a month of groceries, or a head start on your next investment contribution — redirected from airline revenue to your FI journey.

The 7,500-mile rate is available year-round — Turkish doesn't have a separate peak pricing tier for this redemption. But United's saver inventory dries up fast during summer, spring break, and the December holidays. Target September through November and January through mid-February for the best combination of availability and lower cash prices (which tells you demand is lower). Mid-week departures (Tuesday, Wednesday) consistently show better saver seat availability than weekend flights.

Turkish's booking window opens 355 days in advance. United releases the bulk of its saver award inventory when the schedule first opens — roughly 11 months before departure. If you have a specific date in mind (say, a milestone anniversary trip), start checking 355 days out and move fast when you see availability.

Book the outbound through Turkish (LAX→HNL, 7,500 miles) and then search for a separate return award. Turkish allows open-jaw itineraries, so you could theoretically fly into Honolulu and return from Maui if routing works. Piece together two one-way awards for maximum flexibility.

This is the single most common mistake. Points transfers to Turkish are irreversible. If you transfer 7,500 points and then discover saver availability has disappeared, those points are in Turkish's system with no easy path back. Always confirm availability on the Turkish booking portal before initiating any transfer.

Marriott Bonvoy transfers to Turkish at a 3:1 ratio and takes 1–5 days. You'd need 22,500 Marriott points to get 7,500 Turkish miles — a terrible rate. Stick with Citi ThankYou or Bilt at 1:1, both instant.

If you're combining this Hawaii redemption with an international Turkish itinerary, Turkish allows free stopovers in Istanbul on connecting itineraries. That's a separate strategy, but worth knowing as your travel portfolio grows.

Turkish miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Even one small miles transaction — earning or redeeming — resets the clock. Transfer a small batch of points or book a cheap award every few years to keep your account alive.

Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles uses a distance-based award chart that treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. destination. Since flights from the West Coast to Hawaii are under 3,000 miles, they fall into the lowest pricing tier at just 7,500 miles each way. Compare this to United MileagePlus, which charges 22,500 miles each way for the same route through its own program. The Turkish chart effectively gives you a 67% discount for the identical seat on the identical United flight. This pricing anomaly is one of the most valuable in travel rewards and has persisted for years.

Register for a free Miles&Smiles account on the Turkish Airlines website. You will need this account to receive transferred miles and book award flights.

Before transferring miles, verify award space exists. Search on United.com for saver-level award space to Hawaii on your preferred dates. If United shows availability at the saver level, it should be bookable through Turkish.

Transfer Citi ThankYou Points or Capital One Miles to your Turkish Miles&Smiles account at a 1:1 ratio. Allow 24-48 hours for transfers to process. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability.

Log into your Miles&Smiles account and search for your United flight to Hawaii. If the online system does not show the award, call Turkish Airlines customer service to book over the phone. Have your flight details and Miles&Smiles number ready.

After booking, you will receive a Turkish Airlines confirmation. Add your United MileagePlus number to the reservation for elite benefits. You can manage the booking through either Turkish or United once ticketed.

Yes. Turkish Miles&Smiles prices United-operated flights to Hawaii at 7,500 miles each way in economy because its award chart treats Hawaii as a domestic U.S. route. The same seat through United's own program costs 22,500 miles — three times more.

The most practical path is through Citi ThankYou Points, which transfer 1:1 to Turkish Miles&Smiles. The Citi Premier card earns 3x on travel and gas, making it a strong earning tool. Capital One Miles also transfer to Turkish at a 1:1 ratio.

Availability depends on United releasing Star Alliance partner award space (sometimes called "saver" availability). Searching 2-4 months in advance, on weekdays, or during shoulder season (April-May, September-October) significantly improves your chances.

Yes, but the miles cost increases with distance. From the East Coast, flights to Hawaii price at 10,000-12,500 miles each way depending on routing distance. Still an excellent deal compared to United's own pricing, though the West Coast offers the absolute lowest redemption.

This redemption was built for the ChooseFI member who's just starting to take travel rewards seriously — someone who has a Citi credit card, has been accumulating ThankYou Points on everyday spending, and wants their first "I can't believe this worked" moment.

Families planning a Hawaii vacation. At 7,500 miles per person, a family of four needs just 30,000 miles one-way — an achievable balance for anyone who's been strategic with a single Citi card for 6–12 months. The savings versus paying cash for four tickets can easily hit $1,500–$2,000, which is serious FI-community money.

Couples looking for a meaningful but accessible trip. Hawaii is aspirational without requiring long-haul international travel. This is the redemption that converts skeptical partners into believers.

West Coast residents (California, Washington, Oregon, Nevada) who have direct United service to Hawaii from nearby airports. The further you are from direct Hawaii service, the more complex positioning becomes.

Minimum points balance needed: Just 7,500 Citi ThankYou or Bilt points per one-way flight. That's genuinely achievable — even a single welcome bonus on an entry-level Citi card exceeds this threshold.

This redemption is less ideal for travelers on the East Coast (positioning flights eat into the simplicity), anyone without access to Citi or Bilt points (other transfer paths are inefficient), and travelers who need guaranteed availability on specific peak dates — the saver inventory just isn't reliable enough for inflexible itineraries.

This redemption is rated **Easy** in category but carries a few specific friction points worth understanding before you start. The **earning side is straightforward** — 7,500 Citi ThankYou Points is a modest target that most people hit within a few months of regular spending on a Citi Strata Premier. The transfer to Turkish is instant and simple. The **main challenge is availability**. United's saver economy inventory to Hawaii is genuinely limited, especially during popular travel windows. You may search your ideal dates and find nothing. This isn't a bug — it's just the nature of partner award bookings. The program prices this incredibly cheaply *because* the airlines release limited seats at this level. The **booking interface** adds minor friction. The Turkish Miles & Smiles website works, but it's not as polished as booking directly on United.com. Expect a slightly clunky experience — search patiently, and don't be surprised if you need to refresh or try slightly different date combinations. **Three tips to overcome the main challenges:** 1. **Be flexible with dates.** Saver availability is the limiting factor. If you can move your trip by 2–3 days, your chances of finding a seat increase dramatically. 2. **Search early.** Start 10–11 months out. The availability you can't find at 3 months may have been wide open at 11 months. 3. **Confirm before you transfer.** Check the Turkish booking tool *first*, then move your points. This keeps the process clean and stress-free. If you're willing to be slightly flexible on dates, this redemption is genuinely beginner-accessible — and the payoff, especially for a family, makes the modest extra effort completely worthwhile.

The Turkish Miles&Smiles sweet spot for Hawaii flights is one of the most dramatic value plays in travel rewards. Booking the exact same United flight for 7,500 miles instead of 22,500 United miles is a 67% savings, and at cash values of $400-$800+, you are getting 3-5 cents per mile in value. While the booking process can require a phone call and some patience, the savings are substantial enough to make this one of the first sweet spots every travel rewards enthusiast should learn. If you hold Citi ThankYou or Capital One points and want to visit Hawaii, this is your move.

#8920. YSG creates Bali wellness hotel with DJ station

Australian studio YSG has converted a former private vacation residence into a boutique hotel in Bali focused on playful spaces and Indonesian music and culture.

The Moon Gang Bali hotel is located among the rice fields on the northern outskirts of Ubud and includes five interconnected suites, outdoor terraces and a lounge surrounding a central courtyard.

According to its Australian hoteliers, the hotel was inspired by “our feverish obsession with Indonesian music and culture” and its offerings include an all-day spa and a “DIY DJ station” stacked with Indonesian and Japanese city pop records curated by DJ Midnight Runners.

YSG was similarly influenced by Indonesian and Japanese design for the hotel’s spaces, which feature bamboo and timber structures and lava stone tiling.

“Once a private vacation residence in severe disrepair, the concrete bunker was radically transformed into a modern-day Babylon infused with cosmic references and hybrid Japanese architectural elements, including the spa’s sliding bamboo doors depicting lunar phases,” the studio said.

The hotel is only accessible via motorbike or on foot, according to the team, and is located along an alleyway.

Guests enter on the far side of the courtyard pool, while the suites and common areas enclose the space on three sides.

The suites were designed with “dreamers, misfits and wanderers in mind”, according to the hotel, and each is outfitted with an assortment of objects by local studios set against walls clad in recycled earth-based finishes.

Locally made objects throughout the hotel include counter and stools manufactured from recycled plastic bottle tops by Weedoo Plastics, pool lounge chairs handwoven from upcycled materials by BYO Living and wall sconces made of local seseh wood and green-coloured resin by AA Practice.

YSG also made efforts to source construction materials locally while working on the project, as the studio noted it was difficult to transport them to the secluded site.

This included crushing terracotta tiles and breeze blocks and repurposing them as flooding riffraff to help with drainage, and joinery designed to be assembled on site.

The studio also addressed significant water damage to the complex and replaced rotten wooden walls, portions of the roof and concrete flooring.

The project also included adding a second-storey suite made of bamboo with an oversized skylight.

Other details include a black-and-white checkered tile relief that surrounds the pool’s edge, as a nod to the Saput Poleng cloths wrapped around holy objects as part of local customs.

YSG previously converted a warehouse into a co-working space in Sydney and brought 1970s elements to a local cafe.

#8918. 3 Signs You’re the ‘Fringe Friend’ of Your Group, According to a Psychologist

Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because the truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Technically, you’re part of a friend group…well, loosely speaking. You’re in the chats. You receive the invites, but usually ones that sound like “Oh, but you can come if you want”...which, the more you think of it, lands less like inclusion and more like a pity afterthought.

You’re there for big, public-facing plans—birthday parties, girls’ trips, anything that benefits from a larger headcount—yet absent from spontaneous happy hours and nights out where real bonding happens and the inside jokes are born.

If any of this hits close to home, you might be what some people call the backup or “fringe friend.”

We can’t all be everyone’s number one. But what makes this situation so hard is that there’s no obvious villain and no dramatic fallout (which, in some ways, would almost be easier to deal with). Instead, you’re left with a low-grade, hard-to-prove insecurity: Am I just…no one’s first choice? I’m their friend…but are they mine?

For this week’s column, SELF tapped Christina Ferrari, PsyD, a Miami-based psychologist to break down three clear signs you’re a second-tier “backup friend.”

As in, you hear about each plan the day of. You’re added to existing dinner reservations only after somebody else has cancelled. Of course, this might be a matter of logistics or innocent forgetfulness, which is why “every now and then, it’s not cause for concern,” Dr. Ferrari tells SELF. People who are disorganized across the board also exist. “So if this is how they are with all of their friends, that might reflect more about their poor planning”—annoying in its own way, but ultimately a separate issue. The point is, pay attention to the pattern if you can recall more than a few instances.

A few of these tells are subtle yet revealing. Somehow, get-togethers conveniently skip the messy, in-between stage of coordination (“Does 7 work?” “Where should we go?”), arriving at you fully formed. Or, in person, everyone references memes, messages, or memories that clearly happened…just not in any chat you’re in.

“It's totally normal for people to have multiple friendships and separate interactions,” Dr. Ferrari points out. “This isn’t about being included in everything.” Still, paying attention to how often this occurs makes it easier to understand “why you feel like you’re constantly stepping into something already established rather than being part of it from the beginning,” Dr. Ferrari explains.

“Life, of course, can get busy, and a temporary imbalance is normal,” Dr. Ferrari says. But when you’re truly in the crew, your absence will be missed or, at the very least, acknowledged. Someone will notice: “Wait, where have you been?” “I haven’t seen you in forever.” “We never see you anymore.” “Let’s catch up.”

There’s usually, in other words, a small moment of recognition—an indication that you exist in their shared awareness when you’re not physically present, which is why when you don’t get any of those little check-ins, it’s disorienting. It’s as if you’re not important enough to be missed.

Bring it up, and you risk sounding insecure. Say nothing, and you’ll continue to overanalyze every delayed invite, every inside joke, and every Instagram story you weren’t tagged in.

None of the options above sounds appealing. Though if you do want to say something, Dr. Ferrari recommends a low-pressure check-in like: “I always have such a great time when we all hang out. Next time, I'd love to be looped in!” It’s warm, subtle, and assumes good intent—the kind of communication that makes your intentions clear without putting anyone on the defensive. But in ambiguous situations like these—where your gut is whispering that something’s off, yet no one is technically doing you wrong—even the most carefully crafted messages can’t give you the reassurance (or confidence) you’re seeking.

That’s why the solution isn’t necessarily, “How do I become a core member of this group?” Dr. Ferrari says, but instead: “Am I spending my energy where I actually feel like I matter?”

Nobody deserves to feel disposable with people they care about most. And it’s worth remembering that not being fully “in” in one circle doesn’t mean you’re inherently less than, which is where a different solution comes in: Expand your social network instead of over-investing in your current one.

In other words, go out of your comfort zone and start weekly lunches with your favorite coworker. Finally say yes to that old high school companion you’ve been meaning to reach out to but haven’t prioritized. Agree to that weekend trip with friends-of-friends instead of defaulting to your usual group or staying in.

Sometimes, all it takes is noticing the spaces where you’re truly welcome to ease the ache of feeling like the “unimportant” one.

#8915. 7 Subtle Signs You’re Dating for Validation, Not Connection

For a long time, I thought I was doing everything right in dating. After getting out of an eight-year relationship—and then a rebound that emotionally wrecked me in ways I didn’t fully process for at least a couple years—I spent the next few years in a strange in-between.

In theory, I was putting myself out there: going on dates, meeting people, and staying open even when it felt exhausting. But in reality, it felt more like going through the motions, like I was playing a role I had gotten really good at. I had just enough distance to feel in control, but not enough awareness to realize how that distance was shaping my behavior.

But after what felt like an uncountable number of first dates in New York City, I started to notice a pattern: I treated dates like auditions. I would show up polished, engaged, and asking the right questions. If they liked me—texted after, complimented me, and wanted to see me again—I felt this immediate sense of relief, almost like I had passed a test. But that feeling rarely lasted, and more importantly, I almost never stopped to ask myself the most basic question: Did I even like them?

It took me a long time to realize that I wasn’t actually dating for connection—I was dating for validation. And according to therapists, that distinction can be subtle but significant, often showing up in patterns that feel normal on the surface but are actually rooted in the need to feel chosen rather than the desire to truly know someone.

Here are some red flags that indicate you might be seeking companionship for the wrong reasons, according to dating experts.

If your mind tends to jump ahead to what your life would look like in a relationship, how it would feel to have a partner, and how this person fits into that picture, you may be more attached to the idea than the reality. As Moe Ari Brown, LMFT, therapist and Hinge’s in-house Love and Connection Expert explains, genuine interest feels grounded in the person themselves: “You should see them as a whole person, not a flattened version or a fantasy.” When you’re dating for validation, the emotional payoff often comes from imagining being chosen, rather than engaging with who the person sitting across from you actually is.

One of the more confusing dynamics is when everything feels strong while you’re together—conversation flows, there’s chemistry, maybe even a sense of closeness—but that energy doesn’t carry over once you leave. According to Sabrina Romanoff, PsyD, a clinical psychologist and relationship expert in New York City, this can reflect “performative chemistry,” where the connection is heightened in the moment but not supported by real emotional investment. It can feel convincing because the highs are so high, but connection that only exists in person often signals that attention is the driving force.

Opening up is a key part of building intimacy, but when it happens too quickly (read: love bombing and trauma dumping), it can function more as a shortcut than a foundation. Dr. Romanoff notes that oversharing early or rushing emotional and physical intimacy can create the illusion of connection without the substance of it. That early intensity can feel meaningful, but in many cases, it’s less about trust and more about accelerating closeness in a way that delivers immediate validation.

You might text consistently, flirt easily, and maintain a steady stream of communication, but when it comes to actually making plans, things stay vague. “When someone is driven by their ego, they tend to keep people interested by dangling a carrot,” Dr. Romanoff says, pointing to the way some people maintain attention without following through. You might keep the interaction alive because it feels good to be wanted without necessarily working to deepen the connection in a tangible way.

Interest that tends to spike at certain moments (i.e. late at night, when you’re bored, or when you’re craving attention) and then fades just as quickly can be revealing. Dr. Romanoff describes this pattern as fluctuating between “highs and lows,” where engagement is driven more by internal needs than sustained interest in the other person. When connection is the goal, effort tends to be steady; when validation is the goal, it often comes in waves.

If your conversations start to feel interchangeable with the same tone, same questions, and same level of interest across different people, your core goals may be less about building something specific and more about keeping options (and attention) open. Danielle Madonna, LCSW, a psychotherapist in Long Island, notes that this kind of behavior can reflect “a need for widespread validation rather than focused emotional investment.” Instead of getting to know one person more deeply, your focus stays on maintaining multiple streams of attention at once.

There’s a difference between excitement and pursuit. If you notice that your interest peaks when someone is slightly out of reach and then drops once they’re clearly available, it may be the chase (not the person) that’s keeping you engaged. “When enthusiasm diminishes after someone expresses real interest, it can signal that the primary drive may have been validation rather than intimacy,” says Madonna. “In other words, it’s not about connection—it’s about the feeling of being wanted.”

According to Brown, the first step is removing any self-judgment once you acknowledge the pattern. “Wanting to feel affirmed in your dating choices is human,” he explains, and recognizing that can make it easier to shift your behavior without shame. From there, the work becomes more internal than external—getting clear on what you actually want a relationship to feel like rather than focusing on whether someone else chooses you. That might look like asking yourself simple but grounding questions: Do I feel at ease around this person? Am I curious about them? Do I feel like I can be myself, or am I performing? The more you anchor into your own experience, the less power external validation holds.

It can also help to strip away the “audience” in your decision-making. Brown suggests imagining that no one else’s opinion matters (no social validation, no external approval), and then asking yourself whether you’d still be interested in the same people. Often, validation-driven dating shows up as choosing people who look good on paper but don’t feel good in practice. Shifting out of that cycle isn’t about forcing connection where it doesn’t exist—it’s about slowing down enough to notice what’s actually there. And when curiosity starts to replace performance—when you’re genuinely interested in who someone is and not just how they feel about you—that’s usually a sign you’re moving closer to real connection.

#8912. Want to Live Longer? Start Flossing Your Teeth

There’s no shortage of hacks, snacks, and habits that purportedly help you stay healthier for longer. But while we’re busy chasing cutting-edge upgrades—from cold plunges and greens powders to living by the gospel of your Oura ring—we tend to miss out on less sexy yet still powerful tweaks that have been shown to meaningfully move the needle on long-term health.

One such staple is the humble roll of floss, which is probably collecting dust in your medicine cabinet. However, you should probably break it out nightly not just for a brighter, cleaner smile, but to potentially benefit your heart and brain, too.

Keep reading to see why skipping that single strand of string could have consequences that go far beyond tender gums.

If you believe that brushing twice daily will suffice for oral health, you’re in for some sobering news. According to Kami Hoss, DDS, author of If Your Mouth Could Talk: An In-Depth Guide to Oral Health and Its Impact on Your Entire Life, your toothbrush cleans only 60 percent of the surface of your teeth. Read: If you don’t floss, nearly half of your mouth goes uncleaned day after day.

“Flossing is a simple but critical intervention because it disrupts bacterial biofilm between the teeth—areas a toothbrush cannot reach,” adds board-certified periodontist Richard Nejat, DDS. When you floss consistently, you reduce bacterial load, plaque buildup, and gum inflammation—all of which can help keep periodontal disease (a.k.a. gum disease) at bay. And there’s a decent chance you’ll be affected: Per the Cleveland Clinic, about half of adults in the U.S. have some form of gum disease.

The tissue surrounding these small crevices also warrants your full attention. “The sulcus—the shallow groove where your gum meets your tooth—is lined with some of the most permeable tissue in the human body,” Dr. Hoss tells SELF. “It’s richly vascularized, meaning bacteria and whatever compounds we introduce there have a remarkably direct pathway into the bloodstream.” And here’s where the longevity benefits of flossing come into play.

On top of staving off periodontal disease, research shows that regular flossing is associated with reduced risk of dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, and stroke. It can also be an important part of managing diabetes. Meanwhile, poor flossing habits have been associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVD mortality. And according to one study of over 5,000 older adults, never flossing increased mortality risk by 30% compared to flossing daily.

So how can one tiny string make such a big difference in long-term health outcomes? For starters, you have some unfriendly bacteria to contend with. “Porphyromonas gingivalis, which occurs in the mouth, infects the gums and causes gum disease and periodontitis,” says Jennifer Timmons, MD, a longevity physician and the founder of Timmons Wellness. She says that this bacteria is present in atherosclerotic plaque that can plug arteries during a heart attack, while Dr. Hoss adds that it’s also been found in the brain tissue of Alzheimer’s patients. That’s why addressing it at the source matters. “If you don’t floss, [the bacteria] can enter the bloodstream and lead to blood vessel inflammation, damage, and tiny blood clots that could cause heart attacks or strokes in other areas,” Dr. Timmons warns. (She notes that these are correlations, not proven causations, though the associations are strong.)

Flossing also actively helps decrease inflammation in the gums, thereby preventing a cascade of vascular damage throughout the body, Dr. Timmons explains. After all, inflammation is a major driver of not only gum disease but also the chronic conditions listed above. When you don’t floss, inflammation proliferates in the mouth—and it doesn’t stay put. “Chronic gum disease creates a systemic inflammatory burden that touches almost every major disease category,” Dr. Hoss warns. That doesn’t mean flossing is a panacea, but it highlights how interconnected oral health and overall health really are.

If you already floss daily, rest assured that you’re ahead of the game. For the rest of us who skimp here and there—or have yet to make flossing routine, despite the awkward biannual urges from our dentist—now’s a great time to pick up the habit.

Dr. Hoss advises flossing at night rather than in the morning. “You’re sealing your mouth for six to eight hours. Clearing that biofilm before bed matters far more than doing it after breakfast,” he says. He also recommends good old string floss above the likes of picks and water flossers, as neither can get into the nooks and crannies at and below the gumline as efficiently. (If traditional floss is tough to maneuver, these alternatives are still better than skipping it altogether.) As for the right way to floss? “Curve it into a ‘C’ shape around each tooth and use an up-and-down motion,” he shares.

In short, flossing is crucial to maintain oral health, and good oral health has clear downstream effects on the rest of the body. Since heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States—and dementia significantly impacts both quality and length of life —anything that meaningfully reduces risk, even modestly, matters in the longevity conversation. “While flossing alone is not a cure-all for heart or brain health, it is one of the easiest daily habits that can support both oral and overall health,” says Dr. Nejat. All said, flossing might not be revolutionary, but it has surprisingly far-reaching potential.

Picture this: you're stepping off a direct overnight flight at Dublin Airport, passport in hand, ready to spend two weeks exploring Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way — and the transatlantic crossing that would have cost you $600 per seat cost you just 13,000 Avios instead. That's the moment this redemption delivers. For the ChooseFI community, the math here is almost offensive in how good it is. A round-trip economy ticket from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus typically runs $300–$600 per person, and during peak summer travel it can climb even higher. At 13,000 Avios one-way, you're squeezing **2.3 to 4.6 cents per point** out of every Avios you redeem. To put that in perspective, most loyalty program analysts consider 1.5 cents per point a solid redemption. You're potentially tripling that benchmark on what is genuinely one of the easiest award bookings in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The pricing inefficiency here runs deep. British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart** — meaning the price in Avios is determined by how many miles the plane physically flies, not by what the airline thinks the market will bear on that route. The North Atlantic crossing from the U.S. East Coast to Ireland is, by aviation standards, a relatively short haul. Dublin sits closer to Boston than Los Angeles does. That geographic reality, baked into BA's award chart structure, means you pay a "short-haul" price for what most travelers consider a major international trip. Aer Lingus operates modern Airbus A321LR aircraft on these transatlantic routes — a genuine premium product in economy with dedicated transatlantic seating, meal service, and that unmistakably warm Irish hospitality. This isn't a cramped regional jet. You're flying a purpose-built transatlantic cabin at a fraction of the cash cost. For a family of four, this redemption is transformational. At 13,000 Avios per person each way, a family round trip costs 104,000 Avios total — a points balance that's achievable with a single well-timed credit card welcome bonus. The alternative? Dropping $2,400 or more in cash for the same four seats. That's real money that stays in your FI journey.

The core insight here is understanding what British Airways Avios actually prices — and exploiting the gap between that and what the market charges.

BA's Avios program uses a distance-based award chart. Every flight is assigned a price based on the number of miles between the origin and destination, broken into distance bands. The critical band for this redemption is the one covering flights up to approximately 2,000 miles for partner airlines. Boston (BOS) to Dublin (DUB) clocks in at roughly 3,100 miles — but here's where it gets interesting: Aer Lingus prices these transatlantic short-haul routes within a favorable partner tier that makes the Avios cost dramatically lower than you'd ever pay booking directly.

Layer 1 — You're not booking BA flights. You're using BA Avios to book Aer Lingus flights. This distinction is everything. British Airways-operated long-haul flights carry notoriously high fuel surcharges — often $300–$800 or more on top of the Avios cost, which can completely destroy the value of your redemption. Aer Lingus, as a partner airline, charges no fuel surcharges on Avios bookings. You pay the Avios plus modest government taxes and fees, typically $5–$30. That's it.

Layer 2 — Off-peak pricing drops it further. BA Avios has off-peak pricing for Aer Lingus transatlantic routes, and when you travel in shoulder season, the rate can be even more favorable. The ChooseFI community travels smart: avoiding peak summer crowds and booking shoulder seasons isn't just about lower prices, it's about a better experience overall.

Avios are accessible from virtually every major transferable points currency:

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Bilt mean you can search for availability, confirm your seats, then transfer points — no need to speculatively move points weeks in advance. That flexibility is a significant advantage for planning.

One important program nuance: Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. As long as you earn or redeem at least once every three years, your balance stays alive. For most ChooseFI members who hold a Chase or Amex card and regularly earn points, this is a non-issue — but it's worth knowing before you let a balance sit dormant.

Before transferring a single point, verify that award space actually exists on your target dates. Navigate to aerlingus.com and search for flights on your route (Boston, New York JFK, or Chicago ORD to Dublin). Aer Lingus displays Avios availability directly on their website — look for the "Avios" fare option when selecting your flight. This is the cleanest way to confirm seats before committing your points.

Alternatively, log into your British Airways Executive Club account at ba.com and use their award search tool. Search for Aer Lingus flights between your U.S. city and Dublin. The results will show Avios pricing — what you're looking for is the off-peak rate, which will display as lower Avios than the standard/peak option.

Use the BA award calendar view to spot off-peak pricing. Generally, traveling outside of peak summer (late June through August) and major holidays will unlock the best Avios rates. Shoulder seasons — late September through November and February through mid-April — are where the ChooseFI community finds the sweet spot of lower crowds, lower prices, and still-beautiful Irish weather.

Once you've confirmed availability on your target dates, calculate the total Avios needed: 13,000 per person, per direction. For a round trip for two, that's 52,000 Avios. Don't transfer until you're ready to book immediately.

Go to ba.com, log into your Executive Club account, and complete the award booking. You'll pay the Avios balance plus applicable government taxes and fees (typically $5–$30 for Aer Lingus partner bookings — far less than BA's own flight surcharges). Enter passenger details, select seats, and confirm.

BA's booking window opens 355 days in advance — if you want peak-adjacent dates, set a calendar reminder to search as early as possible. If your first-choice dates show no availability, try:

Let's make this concrete. It's late September — shoulder season, the absolute sweet spot for Ireland travel — and you and your partner want a 10-day trip to explore the Ring of Kerry and the Cliffs of Moher.

The Cash Reality: A round trip from Boston to Dublin on Aer Lingus in late September runs approximately $550–$650 per person in economy. For two people, you're looking at $1,100–$1,300 before you've spent a single euro in Ireland. That's real money.

The Avios Reality: 13,000 Avios per person, per direction. Round trip for two:

The CPP Math: At a midpoint cash value of $600 per ticket one-way, you're getting 4.6 cents per Avios — nearly triple what most travel rewards programs consider excellent value. Even at the conservative end ($300/ticket), you're at 2.3 cents per point, still well above average.

What the Experience Looks Like: Aer Lingus operates the BOS–DUB route on the Airbus A321LR — a purpose-built transatlantic narrowbody with a dedicated economy cabin, pull-out meal trays, and proper overhead bin space. The overnight flight departs Boston in the evening and arrives Dublin mid-morning, giving you a full day upon arrival. The crew is warm, the food is solid for economy, and there's no connection in London or Amsterdam burning hours off your vacation.

You land at Dublin Airport refreshed (enough), clear customs quickly through the U.S. preclearance facility — one of only a handful in the world — and you're on the road toward Killarney by noon. Your entire transatlantic crossing cost you about 26,000 Avios and $25 in taxes. The Chase Sapphire Preferred welcome bonus alone is worth 60,000 Ultimate Rewards points. This trip is already nearly free before you've optimized anything else.

Amex Membership Rewards periodically runs a 30% transfer bonus to British Airways Avios. When this promotion is live, your 13,000 Avios only costs you approximately 10,000 Amex points. For a family of four round trip (104,000 Avios), that drops to roughly 80,000 Amex points. Set a Google alert for "Amex British Airways transfer bonus" and strike when it appears — these promotions are time-limited.

BA's award search opens 355 days in advance. If you're targeting travel in late spring (May–early June) before peak summer pricing kicks in, mark your calendar and search the moment the window opens. Award space on direct transatlantic routes gets snapped up quickly at good dates.

BA Avios allows open jaw bookings — meaning you can fly into one airport and return from another at the same Avios price. Book Boston → Dublin inbound and Shannon or Cork → Boston outbound, and now your itinerary naturally flows west to east across the country without backtracking. This is the smart traveler's move and it costs you nothing extra in Avios.

British Airways operates some transatlantic routes with a connection through London Heathrow. The moment you're on BA-operated metal, fuel surcharges of $300–$800+ get added to your booking, completely obliterating the value. Always confirm you're booking Aer Lingus flights (flight numbers beginning with EI) when using this strategy.

Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you've transferred points and haven't yet booked, make sure your BA Executive Club account sees some activity within that window. Even earning a few Avios through a BA partner (a hotel stay, a car rental, a shopping portal purchase) resets the clock.

For earning the Avios you need for this redemption, the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve (transferring Chase UR to BA at 1:1) or any Amex Membership Rewards card give you the most flexibility. Both transfer instantly to BA. If you're starting from zero, a single card welcome bonus of 60,000–100,000 points covers a round trip for one to three people depending on timing.

Aer Lingus joined the Oneworld alliance, which means British Airways Avios can book Aer Lingus-operated flights. Because BA uses distance-based pricing, the relatively short transatlantic crossing from the East Coast to Dublin (roughly 3,000-3,500 miles) prices at just 13,000 Avios each way in economy. Compare this to using American Airlines miles (30,000+ each way) or other programs for the same transatlantic flight. The distance-based chart rewards this specific geography with disproportionately low pricing, creating one of the best-value transatlantic sweet spots available.

Verify that Aer Lingus operates nonstop flights from your departure city to Dublin. The strongest year-round service is from Boston and New York. Seasonal routes may only operate during summer months.

Log into your British Airways Executive Club account and search for flights from your city to Dublin using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for Aer Lingus-operated flights (flight numbers starting with EI). Check flexible dates for the best availability.

Once you find availability, transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant from Chase and Amex.

Complete the booking on ba.com. The total will show 13,000 Avios plus taxes and surcharges (typically $50-$100 each way). Review the total out-of-pocket before confirming to make sure it meets your value threshold.

Add your Aer Lingus or Oneworld frequent flyer number to earn status credits. Remember that Dublin offers U.S. Preclearance for return flights — a significant time-saver. Consider booking accommodations using hotel points for a fully points-funded trip.

Aer Lingus operates nonstop flights from Boston (BOS), New York (JFK), Newark (EWR), Hartford (BDL), Philadelphia (PHL), Washington Dulles (IAD), Chicago (ORD), and other seasonal routes. Boston and New York have the most frequent service year-round.

Aer Lingus awards do carry fuel surcharges, typically $100-$200 round trip in economy. While not zero, this is still dramatically less than the $500-$1,000+ cash fare. The net savings remain substantial despite the surcharges.

Dublin can serve as an excellent gateway to the rest of Europe. Aer Lingus offers connections to many European cities from Dublin, and you can also book separate budget airline flights within Europe. Additionally, Dublin has U.S. Preclearance, meaning you clear customs before your return flight — a rare convenience.

Search on the British Airways website (ba.com) using the "Book with Avios" option. Enter your departure city and Dublin as the destination. Aer Lingus-operated flights will appear alongside any BA-operated options. Availability is best 4-10 months in advance.

This redemption was practically designed for families taking their first international trip on points. The scores tell the story: 5/5 for both Family Friendly and Beginner Friendly. Here's why.

At 13,000 Avios per person per direction, a family of four round trip requires 104,000 Avios — a balance achievable with one or two credit card welcome bonuses. The process of booking is straightforward, the availability is genuinely good (4/5), and there are no complicated routing rules to navigate. If your family has been thinking about Ireland and has a Chase or Amex card with a points balance, this is your gateway.

Couples planning a European trip will find this equally compelling — 52,000 Avios for a round trip for two is a realistic near-term savings goal.

Solo travelers with smaller Avios balances can book one-way legs and mix with other redemptions — fly to Dublin on Avios, return from Lisbon on a separate award, and build a multi-country European trip.

This redemption is not ideal for travelers who are highly inflexible on dates and must travel in peak summer. While availability is good, peak summer award space can be tighter. It's also not the right tool for someone trying to fly business class transatlantic — this sweet spot is economy-class only, and the Aer Lingus business class product ("Business Class" cabin) prices considerably higher.

Minimum to get started: 13,000 Avios for a one-way, 26,000 for a round trip solo. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Bilt points all transfer at 1:1.

This redemption earns its **"Easy" / "Beginner" rating** honestly — and here's specifically why. The three things that make award bookings hard are: earning enough points, finding availability, and navigating a complex booking process. This sweet spot sidesteps all three. **Earning is accessible**: The points requirement (13,000 per direction) is low enough that a single credit card welcome bonus provides multiple round trips. You're not chasing exotic transfer partners or waiting years to accumulate. **Availability is genuinely good**: Aer Lingus releases reasonable Avios award space on their transatlantic routes, especially in shoulder season. You're not fighting for one or two seats on a sold-out flight — the calendar will show multiple options. **Booking is clean and predictable**: The BA website is functional, transfers from Chase and Amex arrive instantly (no speculative transfers required), and Aer Lingus imposes no fuel surcharges on partner bookings. The experience is: search, confirm space, transfer, book. Done. **The one thing to watch**: New members sometimes inadvertently book BA-metal connecting flights instead of direct Aer Lingus flights — and then encounter surprise fuel surcharges. The fix is simple: always verify your flight number starts with "EI" (Aer Lingus) and not "BA." When in doubt, search directly on aerlingus.com first to confirm the flight, then book through BA's award portal. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is an ideal first redemption. The systems are forgiving, the value is immediately obvious, and the destination — Ireland — will make you a believer in the travel rewards lifestyle for years to come.

The BA Avios sweet spot to Dublin on Aer Lingus is one of the most compelling transatlantic redemptions available. At 13,000 Avios each way for a nonstop flight that regularly costs $500-$1,000+ in cash, the value proposition is hard to beat. Even with fuel surcharges of $100-$200 round trip, the total cost of 26,000 Avios plus modest fees dramatically undercuts the cash fare. With four major transfer partners and multiple East Coast departure cities, this sweet spot is accessible and practical. If Europe is on your travel list, Dublin via Aer Lingus should be one of the first routes you explore.

#8909. Single Women Deserve Honeymoons Too—Here’s How to Plan One

I’m on a speedboat whizzing towards my latest vacation destination. As we bounce along, I attempt to take a selfie. The shot I want is the waves, the boats, the islands, but I can’t seem to get the kissing couples out the background. No matter which way I turn, there are honeymooners in my viewfinder. The boat operators and I are the only single people on this vessel. Technically I, too, am a part of a couple—actually, a throuple of single girlfriends heading for an Anguilla getaway. The trip is what I like to call a we-moon.

So often we have our dream destinations on reserve for the day we can go with the person we’ve agreed to spend our life with. There’s the honeymoon and the babymoon, but when do single women get to celebrate life milestones and fulfill the desire for companionship and adventure? That’s the we-moon.

For my most recent we-moon, I was invited to the Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla and joined by two girlfriends. Now, you are probably wondering: What is the difference between this and your average girls trip? Well, similar to a honeymoon or babymoon, a we-moon is taken to celebrate a big life milestone. For me, it was my first book. Single women are so often traveling to celebrate others for their bachelorette or wedding or baby shower. Rarely do we get friends to travel and celebrate something that doesn’t fit into the typical timeline.

That is the purpose of a we-moon. It’s making the phone call to ask your friends to travel and celebrate an achievement with you, just like you do for others. It could be a promotion, a new job, a masters degree, or a book deal.

When crafting the perfect we-moon, there are things to keep in mind to make sure that the trip goes smoothly. I spoke to Joy Harden Bradford, PhD, author of Sisterhood Heals about the best way to pull off a destination celebration with no drama.

“I think having a place where everybody can retreat and have alone time is really good if that is something that the group can do. So private sleeping quarters are important,” she says. “Also having conversations about budget ahead of time. Because some people [might say], ‘Oh, we don't need a five-star hotel. We’re just going to be there to sleep. We’re going to be out.’ And other people are like, ‘No, I like luxury.’ So you don’t want to wait until you get there to find out that there’s a difference in the group about that.”

Another thing you should talk about ahead of time is how many group excursions everyone is down to do. “Because I think for a lot of us, there’s so much going on in our regular life that there’s a lot of expectations for what a vacation should be,” says Dr. Bradford. “‘It’s the one time I get to get away,’ and so people really put a lot on it.”

There are many different vacation styles. We’ve all been on a trip that is overplanned and leaves you more exhausted than when you left. Everyone should discuss what activities they want to do, and a good portion should be optional. For example, we worked on an itinerary with our villa concierge. When it came time to do the private yoga session poolside, some people wanted to rest. So I locked in for a one-on-one session, in which I was able to pay extra attention to modifications and my personal pain points. There were plenty of things that we did together, like an afternoon at the spa, where we all got Anguilla-themed massages, and an excursion across the island in a Jeep to see a different beach. Sometimes you just want to take a nap on vacation, and that is okay.

Me doing yoga with my instructor by the villa pool.

One of the things we did as a group was a margarita-making class. The three of us lined up at the bar of the villa and learned how to properly shake and measure lime juice, orange liqueur, and tequila. Research says that picking up a new skill is good for your brain health. (Although I’m not sure they meant consuming three margaritas in an hour….) The new experience for you can be learning a new sport like pickleball, going to a cooking class, or even playing board games by the beach. This is even better when it becomes a social experiment because even if you fail, you can laugh it off with friends.

What is a girls trip without girl talk? You have to set the mood for conversations. It’s not always a good time to dive deep into your last breakup as you are sitting at a noisy restaurant or relaxing at a spa appointment. But when you are away from your regular routine, there is a great opportunity to open up. “If these are people that you’re actually hoping to grow closer to, then it is important to continue to go deeper with those relationships. And that really requires a lot of vulnerability, which is really hard for people,” says Bradford. “Girls trips really provide a great opportunity and a great backdrop because you are away from your regular routine to maybe get into some of those things that you don’t have time to talk about later.” You have to set the mood for your friends to unravel. For me, I planned a night in the villa's private jacuzzi tub, watching the sunset, and drinking wine. That’s where we shared our work woes and dating troubles as a night cap.

My friends and I having girl talk by the fire.
