#8795. Trek’s New Domane Trades IsoSpeed for Wider Tires. I Think It Works

After riding the $11,499 SLR, I think the $4,200 SL 6 AXS is the smartest buy.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

This Review Continues for MembersMy full test and verdict are here. Next, I want to hear what you think. Bicycling members can continue the discussion with me on Discord, where I’ll answer questions and hear how the Domane works for riders beyond my test. The invitation appears after the review.

If you want a comfortable, relatively upright road bike for rough pavement, long rides, and some light gravel, the new Domane belongs on your list. It feels more eager under power than previous versions, while keeping the stability and confidence that have always made the bike good at everyday riding.

The version I’d point most people toward is the $4,200 SL 6 AXS. It gets the same geometry, tire clearance, and basic frame features as the expensive SLR models, along with electronic shifting and carbon wheels. The SLR saves weight and opens the door to Trek’s Project One customization. Those are real advantages, but they don’t make it a fundamentally different bike.

I tested the $11,499 SLR 9 AXS 2x. It weighed 16.3 pounds in size M. The bike I’d recommend first costs less than half as much.

BIKE TESTED: Trek Gen. 5 Domane SLR 9 AXS 2xACTUAL WEIGHT 16.3 pounds (Size M, as tested) USE Road, light gravel PRICE AS TESTED $11,499 MODEL PRICE RANGE $2,400 to $11,499; $14,999 limited edition ICON No. 76FRAME ONLY OPTION: Yes. $3,700 (SLR) $2,000 (SL)CUSTOMIZABLE BUILDS Yes, SLR models through Project One SIZES OFFERED XS, S, M, ML, L, XL WEIGHT LIMIT 125 kg/275 lb (bicycle, rider, and cargo) TIRE CLEARANCE 40mm BB STANDARD T47 threaded BRAKE HOSE ROUTING Internal, RCS headset; under bar/stem on most buildsDRIVETRAIN COMPATIBILITY 1x and 2x, electronic shifting only DERAILLEUR HANGER UDH WARRANTY Lifetime, frame and rigid fork, original owner CRASH REPLACEMENT Yes, Trek Carbon Care discounted replacement

I’ve ridden every generation of the Domane, including several of the more aggressive RSL versions. Over the years, Trek added adjustable IsoSpeed, front IsoSpeed, internal storage, aero shaping, and hidden cables. The fifth-generation bike pulls back on much of that.

The Gen 5 feels more solid and reactive underfoot than its predecessors. It’s stiffer when I get on the pedals, accelerates with more snap, and climbs with a crispness that used to elude the Domane. In that way, it feels more like a Madone than any previous version.

It hasn’t lost the stability and confidence that make the Domane a good everyday road bike. I can push it hard down a descent without feeling like I’m taking a test of nerves. The fit is excellent, too. The taller front end should help more riders find a position that’s comfortable and aerodynamic.

And no, it doesn’t feel slow on 35mm tires. The bike feels quick and responsive. The wider tires are part of what makes it work, not an anchor holding it back.

The original Domane’s signature feature was IsoSpeed, a mechanism that let the seat tube flex to add comfort. Trek developed it over several generations, then removed it from the bike that introduced it.

The new Domane gets much of its comfort from wider tires at lower pressures, along with frame and seatpost tuning. Most models come with 35mm tires, and the frame clears up to 40mm. Trek says that combination provides enough comfort that IsoSpeed’s remaining benefit isn’t worth its weight and complexity.

IsoSpeed still works. Trek told me that with the same 35mm tires, the Gen 4 transmits slightly less vibrational energy than the Gen 5. Trek also says the Gen 5 on 35mm tires comes within 5 percent of the Gen 4 on its stock 32mm tires at the rear. At the front, Trek says the two generations perform similarly.

Those are Trek’s test results, not measurements I made. But the decision makes sense to me. Wider tires add traction and capability that IsoSpeed couldn’t provide. Trek decided the system’s remaining comfort advantage wasn’t enough to justify keeping it.

If you own an older Domane, what did IsoSpeed do for you? Did you notice a difference when you moved to wider tires, or do you miss the old system? I’d like to hear what you’ve felt on real roads.

According to Trek’s white paper, the Gen 5 frame is about 292 grams lighter than Gen 4. It also eliminates IsoSpeed and its associated maintenance.

The frame uses a threaded T47 bottom bracket, a round fork steerer, a Universal Derailleur Hanger, and a standard 27.2mm seatpost. For a modern performance bike, there’s not much proprietary weirdness here. That’s a feature.

The internal storage compartment is gone, too. I’ll miss it. It was useful. Trek says its research showed that many Domane owners weren’t using it. The new frame retains fender mounts, top-tube mounts, and frame-bag mounts. I like the trade: less hardware and complexity, with straightforward ways to carry gear when you need to.

The cable routing is another smart compromise. On most models, brake hoses run beneath the two-piece bar and stem before entering the frame at the headset. It looks clean, but changing a bar or stem doesn’t become a major repair job. Fit changes and service matter more to me than hiding every cable at any cost.

The SL and SLR share the same geometry, tire clearance, seatpost size, bottom bracket, UDH, and general feature set. The SL uses Trek’s 500 Series carbon; the SLR uses lighter 900 Series carbon. Trek says both frames are designed to the same stiffness requirements. The SL supports mechanical drivetrains; the SLR is electronic-shifting only.

The SLR primarily buys lower weight, access to Trek’s highest-end builds, and the ability to customize components through Project One. Buyers can specify details such as crank length, handlebar width, and stem length. If you’re spending this much on a bike, getting those dimensions right from the factory is a meaningful advantage.

But the SLR doesn’t change the core experience enough to be the obvious choice for most riders. I’d look closely at the $4,200 SL 6 AXS first. It has a carbon frame, electronic shifting, carbon wheels, 40mm tire clearance, and the same accessible fit. The carbon range starts at $2,400 with the Tiagra SL 4. The SLR 9 AXS 2x I tested costs $11,499.

Trek also offers an ultralight SLR 9 AXS 1x with 28mm tires. Trek describes it as the racier interpretation of the Domane, but it did not vibration-test that configuration. If comfort is a big reason you’re considering the bike, pay attention to the tire setup, not just the frame name.

If you’re shopping for a Domane, which versions are you weighing? Would you spend more for the SLR’s lower weight and Project One options, or put that money toward another bike or gear?

Trek says it applied aero lessons from the Gen 8 Madone, but aerodynamics weren’t a major priority. In a pedaling-mannequin test, Trek claims the Gen 5 improved by 0.6 watts over Gen 4.

That seems appropriate. Trek prioritized weight, simplicity, and ride quality instead of chasing another aero headline.

The fifth-generation Domane is an excellent road bike. It’s light, comfortable, stable, and lively. It’s easier to adjust and service than many integrated performance bikes, retains useful mounts, and drops features that added weight and complexity without improving the bike enough to justify them.

The old Domanes were more technically adventurous. I miss that part of the story more than I miss riding them.

For most riders, I think Gen 5 is the right Trek road bike. The SL 6 AXS is the model I’d point people toward first. The SLR makes sense if you want the lighter frame and factory customization, but the expensive build doesn’t change the core experience. Taken as a whole, the new Domane is my favorite drop-bar bike Trek makes.

That’s my take after riding the bike. Now I want to hear from people who own a Domane, have ridden an earlier version, or are considering the Gen 5. What questions do you still have? What would you like me to investigate or compare? I’ll continue the conversation on Discord and bring the most useful questions and experiences back here.

What do you think of the new Trek Domane? What questions do you still have? What did I screw up? If you own or have ridden the Gen 5 Domane, share your impressions.

Bicycling members can join me in The Test Ride on Discord to continue this review. The invitation is below.

Find the Trek Gen 5 Domane post in the bike-reviews forum. Tell me what you ride and what you’re deciding between. Your feedback and insights will help me write better reviews.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. #8794. This Yoga Video on YouTube Is My Go-To Practice For Lower Back Discomfort

Laura Harold is a Yoga Journal editor who has practiced yoga for more than 10 years. Throughout her years as an editor in the health and wellness space, she’s spent a tremendous amount of time uncovering videos on floor stretches for lower back pain on YouTube. You can explore more yoga poses to help relieve back discomfort.

I often avoid my yoga mat as if I’m playing the “floor is lava” game from childhood. That’s typically due to my default state of caffeinated hyperactivity, wherein I’d rather scrub the baseboards and research water filters than slow down and ground myself for a few minutes. But as someone who’s experienced debilitating lower back pain on and off since I was a kid, I realized that sometimes there’s another reason for my avoidance.

Debating whether to stretch while experiencing pain can feel like a catch-22. The last thing I want to do after triggering my injury is over-stretch and incite more pain. But I’ve learned that after one to two days of requisite rest, the discomfort will circle back with a vengeance if I return to desk-sitting, driving, and couch-surfing without moving my body at least a little.

I’ve tried to search YouTube “gentle lower back yoga,” but I’ve either gotten overwhelmed by the thousands of options or, after finally choosing one and starting a practice, been disappointed by the seemingly inevitable cue to come into Down Dog or Cobra or some other pose that I knew my body wasn’t ready to try. Until the thought occurred to me that maybe “gentle yoga” wasn’t a specific enough search for me.

I did some more digging, instead searching “yoga for older adults,” and came across this 16-minute practice. I didn’t quite realize what I had been missing in the other videos until I experienced this one. The sequence moves at a slow pace, and includes clear and specific cues for mostly reclining postures that can be dialed back if needed, depending on how I’m feeling. For instance, if I’m tending to intense lower back pain, I usually avoid the supine spinal twists in favor of a few Windshield Wipers.

There’s also something about the moments of silence the instructor offers throughout that allow me enough space to hear my own thoughts and determine whether I’m feeling enough of a stretch, too much of a stretch, or need to skip it altogether. Some days, the few core-strengthening exercises in the video are just what I need to feel more supported in my lower back. Other days, I opt to close my eyes and take a few deep breaths instead, which feels equally important.

I think the biggest relief I’ve experienced after finding this practice wasn’t even physical. It was the mental burden it took away—namely, endlessly scrolling videos and debating whether I should even tempt fate by moving my lower back too soon. I’m all too familiar with that dreaded post-injury feeling of knowing that my body needs to move but wondering, “Where do I even begin?” Lately, this practice has been my starting point.

#8793. Does Running Build Muscle?

You know running builds endurance. Here’s how it can change your body composition.

Running obviously builds your endurance. While one mile (or five miles) might feel really hard when you first start running, those distances become much easier the more you get out there.

Running also builds strength. As you power up hills or hit a finishing kick, you realize you have the force required to pick up the pace.

But does running build muscle? Can you change your body composition simply by clocking more miles?

The short answer is yes. But there’s more to the story. Here’s what to know about running and its affect on muscle mass.

Research shows running can produce muscle growth. For example, a 2015 research review, published in the journal Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews, found that aerobic exercise can increase skeletal muscle and whole muscle size, particularly in sedentary individuals. (This means those just starting to run are more likely to experience the muscle-building benefits.) Those study authors suggest aerobic exercise as a mechanism to stave off the muscle loss that comes with aging.

Likewise, a 2017 study published in the International Journal of Exercise Science found that running induced muscle growth in the vastus lateralis muscle (one of the quadricep muscles) in 12 recreationally active university students. The participants completed about 25 sessions of high-intensity running (four sets of four minutes of running at 90 to 95 percent of heart rate max, with three minutes of active rest in between) for 10 weeks.

This muscle growth likely stems from the way running loads the body—more specifically, the lower body. “With running, the majority of the muscle work or contraction is eccentric, which is the hardest load on the body,” Joe McConkey, a Boston-based exercise physiologist and USATF-certified running coach tells Runner’s World. Eccentric contractions occur when a muscle lengthens under load or tension. For example, during the lowering phase of a squat, the quadriceps (front of thigh) muscles eccentrically contract.

When running, “the act of landing, where you’re absorbing two to four times your body weight, is done eccentrically. That’s the major stimulus for muscle growth during running, particularly for beginners,” McConkey says.

Recent research shows that aerobic exercise may have more of an effect on maintaining muscle mass, rather than building it. That’s especially true if you stick to a similar routine, without adding intensity.

That said, new runners, compared to those who have been running for a while, are more likely to see the most noticeable changes in muscle mass and strength just by virtue of running more often or for longer for the first time (or the first time in a long time).

Also, even though runners who consistently do steady-state runs won’t build more muscle mass, their muscles can start to look more defined as body composition changes due to increasing mileage, adds McConkey.

If you’ve been running a long time, you’ve also probably already built strength in the slow-twitch muscle fibers that primarily power your long distance running, Janet Hamilton, C.S.C.S., owner of Running Strong, tells Runner’s World.

All runners can develop more strength—in terms of power and muscle ability—and likely more muscle by tapping into their fast-twitch muscle fibers, which have less endurance than slow-twitch fibers but exert more force. “These don’t really get called upon until either a) there’s an activity that requires more strength than slow-twitch fibers can muster or b) the slow-twitch fibers are fatigued and you keep going,” says Hamilton.

To recruit more of those fast-twitch fibers, you need to do something that requires greater power output. Think about the massive leg muscles of a sprinter: “Any high-powered, short bout of exercise—so long as it is progressive in nature (i.e. harder, faster, higher than what you have already adapted to)—will increase the size of fast-twitch fibers, and thus increase muscle mass,” says McConkey.

In summary, to promote muscle growth, you need a bigger challenge on your muscles and a variety of challenges, otherwise running will offer more maintenance than progression.

To support your muscle-building efforts, consider the general exercise recommendations for each week: at least three cardio workouts, two strength workouts, and at least one flexibility workout. Incorporating these all into your routine will not only support your muscles, but make you a more well-rounded athlete.

One crucial component of that muscle-building plan is weight training. Strength workouts create micro-tears in your muscles that, during recovery, build back bigger and stronger. You also need enough protein in your diet to help with this process.

When it comes to running, though, an easy way to build fast-twitch fibers and muscle mass is through hill workouts. “Running up a hill requires more muscle power than running on level ground,” says Hamilton. You may not be lifting a weight, but you’re carrying your own weight up an incline against the force of gravity—its own kind of resistance training.

Speed workouts will also engage fast-twitch muscle fibers. “If you’ve been doing nothing but easy effort, marathon-pace runs, incorporating short to moderate intervals at a faster, 5K pace is going to require you to exert more force every time your foot hits the ground,” says Hamilton. “And that’s how you speed up—you generate a greater push-off.”

To build more muscle on your runs, check out these workouts below. The mileage, effort, and total distance will depend on your running fitness, but each workout can be scaled up or down to meet you where you are in your training.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a new runner who has been exercising regularly for at least a year, or someone who has completed a few 5Ks or 10Ks and can complete 6 miles in one workout. This plan peaks at 28 miles in a week with a 12-mile long run.

John Vasudevan, M.D. is an associate professor at the University of Pennsylvania. He is board-certified in Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation and Sports Medicine. He is a Team Physician for UPenn Athletics and  medical director of the Broad Street Run and Philadelphia Distance Run, and previously for the Rock 'n' Roll Half-Marathon and Tri-Rock Triathlon in Philadelphia. He sees patients at the Penn Medicine and the Philadelphia Veterans Administration hospital. He has been in practice at the University of Pennsylvania since 2012.

#8791. 4 Winter Running Habits to Keep Building Endurance in the Off-Season—No Treadmill Required

Expert-backed ways to maintain your aerobic fitness when cold weather tests your routine.

When days get shorter, temperatures get colder, and you no longer have a race on the horizon, the motivation to run consistently can seriously start to wane.

But prioritizing your aerobic fitness all year means you don’t have to start from scratch when it comes time to train for a race again, says Brant Stachel, an Ontario-based USATF-certified endurance coach at Fast and Free Performance Coaching. “Anytime you’re taking big swaths of time off, you have to go back into rebuilding mode where you spend weeks getting back up to the fitness that you previously had,” he says.

Whether you’re a longtime treadmill hater in need of more exciting options or you simply don’t have access to one, we tapped experts for their best alternatives that allow you to maintain your endurance without hopping on the belt. Follow these habits to keep your aerobic engine revved in the off-season.

The minimum amount of training you need to do depends on your fitness level and your current (or most recent) training load. “If you’re somebody who’s running five to seven days a week, you probably still want to do three to four days a week,” Stachel suggests.

Even one to two days a week can keep you from starting completely from scratch in the spring season, says Danielle Kroot, DPT, certified run coach and physical therapist based in Portland, Maine. “It’s also keeping your tissues and muscles exposed to that type of load so that there’s not this shock to your system when you start training for a race again, and can help decrease injury risk,” she adds.

Keep in mind it usually takes six weeks of consecutive low-mileage weeks to really lose fitness gains, says Andrea Dell, an RRCA-certified run coach, so taking a few weeks off (especially if you’re recovering from marathon season) won’t do any harm; it’ll actually help you recharge.

Unless you’re training for marathons year-round, you’re likely periodizing your training, Stachel says, which means cycling through off-seasons, shorter distances, and maintenance mode in between major race training cycles. He explains that periodizing your training is really important for staying well-rounded and building adequate speed, strength, and endurance—all factors that make you a stronger, faster runner.

Winter is a great time to analyze any gaps or weaknesses in your fitness, especially following a fall marathon season, Stachel says. Look at your recent training cycles and factor in what didn’t work for you. You might address strength and injury prevention after dealing with nagging calf pain, or consider focusing on speed workouts you didn’t get to hit as much during a marathon season, like mile race pace, 3K, and 5K pace efforts, he adds.

Strength work builds stability, power, and durability for better performance, and can help you handle mileage and speed. Building more strength in the off-season will translate to more speed, power, and injury prevention when you decide to ramp mileage back up.

Off-season strength should generally target major muscle groups runners rely on most, like the calves, glutes, and quads. Both Dell and Kroot recommend focusing on deadlift variations, squat variations, lunges, calf raises, step-ups, and plyometric movements.

Generally, you want to choose weights that make you feel like you could do only two more repetitions; that signals that the weight is heavy enough, Kroot explains.

“Even if you’ve got those five-pound weights hanging out in your basement, you can see how many squats you can do until you feel close to exhaustion,” Stachel adds.

If you have limited equipment at home, each expert recommends combining movements, such as doing a 15-minute stair climb, followed by bodyweight burpees or planks.

One particularly snowy winter, Stachel broke up his 90-minute run into five different sections, utilizing the equipment at his local gym and combining running and cross-training in one session. He ran 15 minutes to his local gym, went on the elliptical for 20 minutes, biked for 20 minutes, went on the treadmill for 20 minutes, then ran 15 minutes home. “The idea of simply going on a treadmill for 90 minutes was mentally numbing,” he says.

Stachel explains that while it’s best to complete a 90-minute run through running alone to stay specific to your sport, you have to find a workout you can stick with. “The best winter workout is the one you’ll actually repeat and build on next week,” he says.

In the off-season, cross-training is your friend, Stachel says. Even if you don’t have any injuries, it’s a good idea to add some form of alternative aerobic-focused movement to your routine such as swimming, aqua jogging, elliptical, or cycling. “Then it doesn’t seem like a shock to the system when that first snowfall drops and you’ve got a week where you can’t go outside and run,” he adds. Stachel explains that gym memberships can be especially helpful for this reason.

Stachel’s go-to workout: a tempo session on the elliptical. “This has the closest carryover to running in terms of cardiovascular function,” he says. “It also loads the tissues because you’re more upright, whereas on the bike you don’t get that.”

You can do any run interval workout on the elliptical or another cross-training machine, Stachel says, but the general rule is to take your typical outdoor recovery time and cut it in half. For example, if you give yourself two minutes to recover between tempo intervals outside, take one-minute recoveries on the elliptical. This might look like three 10-minute bouts at tempo pace with one minute of easy efforts in between.

If you don’t typically go to a gym, Dell and Kroot recommend stair workouts, at-home workout videos that provide follow-along Zumba or high-intensity interval workouts, and jumping rope.

Each expert recommends making an effort to still get outside as much as possible, even if it’s once or twice a week, or more during weeks when your local weather cooperates. Bundling up for the occasional outdoor run keeps training exciting, and helps your body stay adjusted to the roads.

Here are a few of their tips for making the most of those outdoor runs.

Oftentimes the best way to stay consistent with running in the off-season is to find safe, paved places to run when roads might be wet or covered in snow. Stachel recommends asking other runners in your community or talking to runners at your local run store to find the best routes in your area.

“Every city I’ve been to or coached in during the winter has had some hidden gem that’s plowed for some reason,” Stachel says. This might be a municipal building, a local mall, hospital, or other parking lots. “Those little tips and tricks can make it all the more fun,” he adds.

Good gear becomes your armor for bracing cold winter runs. “If you’re out there and you’re underdressed, you’re miserable the entire time. If you’re overdressed, then you’re sweating through your clothes and your heart rate’s high and then you’re frustrated,” Dell says.

To dress according to winter weather, use the Runner’s World what to wear tool, which shows you how to layer based on different weather patterns. Dell also recommends investing in a good pair of fleece-lined tights or joggers, as well as ear covers and gloves. Stachel also recommends microspikes that you can strap onto running shoes for better traction on wet or snowy surfaces.

View the off-season as an opportunity to rise to another challenge, Stachel says. “There are so many times that as athletes, we feel hardcore for doing things. You could probably figure out a way to feel really hardcore for navigating a crazy winter or running,” he says, noting that a sense of empowerment comes from training through a season that many people don’t train through.

“Winter doesn’t change what builds endurance, it just changes how you collect it,” says Stachel. You might spend more time hacking your training and moving workouts indoors, or bundling up to run outside.

By spring, you can expect an “epic” racing season that feels rewarding and full of satisfaction because of all the hard work you put in during winter months, Stachel notes. Then, you will likely find the urge to continue training every winter because you know you’ll feel rewarded when the spring comes and you’re much closer to hitting your paces and PRs.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#8788. Wiz Khalifa Just Ran His First 5K—and His Time Was Surprisingly Fast

The rapper made his debut at Diplo’s Run Club in Los Angeles on Sunday.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Wiz Khalifa has never been particularly shy about his love of smoking weed, but lately, he's been chasing a different kind of high. On Sunday, November 8, the "Black and Yellow" rapper made his 5K debut at Diplo's Run Club in Los Angeles, clocking 22:55 at an average pace of 7:23 per mile. He finished 95th among 10,991 participants, which is quite the racing debut for someone who only started getting serious about the sport a few months ago.

And to think his whole running obsession started with what was supposed to be a simple walk.

In an October interview with Hypebeast, Khalifa explained that he’d gone out to a trail one day, decided to pick up the pace, and eventually checked his watch to discover he’d gone four miles. And to his surprise, he also realized he’d accidentally discovered a new hobby.

"Oh sh*t! I kind of liked that," he recalled.

Apparently, that was enough to get him investing in proper shoes and gear, and by July, he was documenting his workouts on social media, telling his Instagram followers how much he enjoyed getting out there with increasingly ambitious mileage goals (and even catching Strava's attention when the platform offered to help verify his account). More recently, he challenged himself to cover 30 miles in a week, telling fans, "You can join in or watch me be great."

Of course, given Khalifa's well-documented relationship with marijuana, there's an obvious question about how all this cardio is treating him. He certainly doesn't seem too concerned.

"My lungs are holding up great. I'm getting faster," he told Hypebeast, crediting his years of Muay Thai training and performing onstage for his endurance.

Whatever his routine, Khalifa certainly had plenty of energy left after Sunday's 5K. In a post-race Instagram video, he's seen enjoying every second of his new racing career, bouncing around, dancing, and proudly showing off his Strava results.

And as for his post-race celebration? He wound up in Diplo's DJ booth, of course.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#8786. This Seated Twist Stretches Your Spine, Engages Your Core, and Enhances Your Awareness

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about a seated twist first appeared in the March-April 1994 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

To encourage new perceptual skills in my students, I like to ask them from time to time to practice in a new spot in the yoga studio. If you’re like most people, after a few classes you find yourself regularly gravitating to the same location, often within a few inches of accuracy.

The mere suggestion to place your mat in the front of the room instead of the cozy corner may make you decidedly un-comfortable. Changing positions enables you to see yourself and the world from a different vantage point, much as a photographer might circle a subject to get pictures from different angles.

It’s not surprising, considering the propensity of our species to form habits, that we tend to perceive our bodies from one perspective, including some aspects of ourselves while leaving others out.

Thus our perception of our body may become like a two-dimensional sketch, deprived of the volume, form, and texture that would extend our awareness into the three-dimensional realm. While Eastern cultures have investigated and honored the inner layers of the body as the key to our physical, mental, and spiritual health, most Western cultures have concerned themselves primarily with the body’s superficial layers. Because of this bias, most of us have come to view our movements as entirely dictated by the muscles and bones, unconsciously deleting other systems from our awareness. Keeping the mind on the outer layers, we become unable to feel or act from our deeper selves.

One of the body systems that brings us most succinctly into a deeper sense of self are the organs, the contents of the musculoskeletal container. Awareness of the organs gives our movements volume, form, and a sense of ripe fullness. Through the health and vitality of the organs, the outer layers gain their strength and form.

Just as we might bring our attention to the sensation of a muscle stretching, we can bring our attention to the sensation of an internal organ. When we change the vantage point of our awareness to bring the inner body into the foreground (an inner adjustment analogous to moving to a different place in the yoga studio), the way we experience ourselves and the quality of our movement will be quite different.

For most of recorded history, yogis have been engaged in just this kind of research, exploring the effects that the asanas (as well as pranayama and meditation) have on the deeper, subtler bodily systems. The ancient practitioners noted which movements and practices stimulated, purified, sedated, or neutralized the energy currents moving deep within the body, correlating these phenomena to health, longevity, and the elevation of consciousness. By contrast, they were not terribly interested in the state of their hamstring muscles, and traditional texts make few references to such structures.

Movements that twist the body compress, elongate, and massage the inner organs. Unfortunately, twists are often practiced exclusively from the perspective of the musculoskeletal system; we use the strength of the muscles and the leverage of the bones to force the body into rotation without ever inviting the soft inner contents along for the ride. Focusing on the internal organs not only reduces the possibility of injury, but stimulates and tones these deep structures by bringing our attention to them, just as electrical activity is created in our muscles simply by visualizing them flexing.

In this article, we’re going to look at how changing the vantage point of our awareness affects the practice of Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi (Marichyasana III), a seated twist.

Bringing attention to the inner body is a way to physically organize our presence on this center. Knowing that there is nowhere to “get to,” we can proceed with the full knowledge that we are on our way.

The following exercise was adapted from Sensing, Feeling, and Action by Bonnie Bainbridge Cohen. Sit on a cushion or blanket with your legs crossed. Close your eyes and let yourself settle. Bring your awareness to the soft inner contents of the torso surrounded by the musculoskeletal container. Imagine your body as two concentric cylinders with the soft internal organs on the inside and the harder musculoskeletal system surrounding them. Feel how the rise and fall of the breath swells from the core and communicates itself to the outer layer.

Now gently bring your awareness to each of your major organs. In the chest is the heart, slightly to the left of center, with the lungs on either side. In the upper left quadrant of the abdomen is the stomach; in the upper right quadrant of the belly is the liver, which extends up underneath the rib cage. The small intestines occupy most of the central and lower belly. In the lower right quadrant of the belly, the small intestine becomes the large intestine, which makes a hairpin turn to run up the right side of the belly (the ascending colon), across the top (the transverse colon), and down the left side (the descending colon), finishing as the sigmoid colon and rectum.

You may want to refer to an anatomy text for a more in-depth discussion of the internal organs. For now, sense their general position and volume, using your breath to palpate them. The kidneys lie on either side of the spine above the waist. The uterus is deep in the abdomen above the pubic bone.

Now bring your attention to your skeletal structure, as if you were seeing the body with X-ray vision. Extend your right arm over your head and bend to the left, focusing your attention on the bones moving. Repeat this to the other side.

Returning to the first side, initiate the side bend from the skeleton and then Shift your attention to the underlying organs, focusing on elongating the organs on the right side of the body and compressing the organs on the left. Did you go further? How did the quality of the movement change as your focus shifted?

Now initiate the side bend as a movement that arises from the organs. Breathe into and elongate the organs on the right side of the body, letting the skeleton follow. How did this experience differ from the one in which you had your mind on the skeletal system alone?

The organs are the seat of our deepest emotions; we physically experience strong feelings as sensations in the viscera (for example, the butterflies of fear or the tight knot of anger). Therefore, many people find that when they initiate movement from the organ system, the movement seems to arise out of their deepest self—that is, there is not a dualistic sense that the mind is “doing something” to the body. By contrast, when you perceive the body as nothing but a skeleton, it may feel as though your mind is manipulating your body like a puppet on a string.

Now integrate this new awareness of your organs into a simple twisting posture.

Some preliminary suggestions may make your task easier. One of the obstacles to twisting freely is the inability to sit upright with the normal curves of the spinal column intact. When the legs are extended, this problem may be further exaggerated because the hamstrings may pull on the base of the pelvis, causing the back to round (Figure 1: Incorrect). In this position, you are actually sitting on the base of the spine rather than on the sitting bones, and the collapse of the outer body makes it difficult to breathe freely.

To make sitting—and therefore twisting—a little easier, this first variation calls for both legs to be folded. By deactivating the hamstrings, we allow the pelvis to move more freely into an upright position.

Sit cross-legged with the buttocks elevated on a blanket or cushion. Place the right leg so the shin is upright, with the sole of the right foot directly in front of the left ankle. Inhaling fully, allow the abdomen to expand freely. On your exhalation roll the abdomen to the right, guiding the abdomen back against the spine to encourage the twist. Bring your left elbow onto the outside of the right knee (Figure 2).

With each breath, allow the soft inner body to move circularly in the direction of the twist, very much as if you were doing a belly dance. Once the lower torso is turning freely to the right, direct the breath more fully into the right side of the chest. Expanding the right lung with the inhalation, encourage the thoracic spine to move in and up. As you exhale, release the left lung from the center of the chest out into the shoulder, allowing the muscles along the back of the body to follow the changing shape of the lung.

As this occurs, the shoulder blade and then the arm will move further around.

Replace the elbow against the knee as necessary. When you feel you have reached your limit, stay for a few more breaths, simply letting the inhalation and exhalation oscillate the body slightly to and fro. Release on an exhalation and then repeat on the other side.

Now extend both legs in front of you, placing a blanket underneath your buttocks if necessary to create an erect sitting position. Sit with your back one arm’s length from a wall. Bend your right knee, placing the heel of the right foot in line with the sitting bone of the right side of the pelvis. Extend downward through the length of the left leg, simultaneously pressing the right foot down into the floor. Feel how this groundedness through the bones rebounds up through the body as the energy flows through the soft organs and the bones to support the erect carriage of the torso. When you release the downward movement of the legs, notice how the spine sags and the whole torso wilts.

Sense how the movements of the muscles and bones affect the shape of the internal organs, and vice versa.

As you inhale, direct the breath into the mid and upper chest. With each exhalation, successively turn from the lowest part of the belly to the head. Bring your elbow onto the outside of the right knee and place your hand against the wall, making sure that you are far enough from the wall that the shoulder is not elevated toward the ears (Figure 3). Use your arm to lift and support the torso, but do not overpower the soft movements of the inner body by using the arm to forcefully turn the outer muscles. Instead of using the arm as a “dictator,” let your arm become a “guide.” In the same way, wait for the inner body to yield to the movement, then encourage it with the guiding arm.

Take a few more full breaths before releasing and repeating the movement on the second side.

In this exercise you will focus on the contents of the spine—the spinal cord—to bring deeper awareness to your movement. Begin by sitting in Staff Pose (Dandasana) with both legs extended. Bend the left knee and place the heel of the left foot in line with the sitting bone. Now place the left hand immediately behind the left buttock and use it to support the trunk.

Before beginning the twist, take a moment to bring a few central images to mind. Start by bringing your awareness to the contents of the skull. Sense whether the brain is balanced equally between the front and back of the skull. Exiting the brain is the brain stem; then the spinal cord runs through each vertebrae like thread running through a string of beads.

Think of your spinal cord as the tail of your brain and the vertebrae as individual beads, each with its own size and shape.

As you bring your awareness to the brain stem, notice how the spinal cord curves inward so that the cervical vertebrae stack up underneath the head. As you continue your mental journey down the back, the soft spinal cord curves outward, following the convex curve of the thoracic spine. As you move your attention down toward the base of the rib cage, the spinal cord loops back in and the five lumbar vertebrae stack directly under the center of the chest. Continue on down to the massive sacral bone which curves outward and articulates with the two wings of the pelvis.

Having established this anatomical map, begin to sense how the bones of the spine are positioned in relationship to the soft spinal cord. Are there any areas of the spinal cord that feel compressed, perhaps even red and sore from being pressed and rubbed by the bodies of the vertebrae? Are there vertebrae that feel as if they were glued together, or areas where the bones feel rotated or collapsed on one side? Use your breath to gently move your vertebrae as if you were rearranging very precious antique furniture in a room. Adjust the vertebrae so they glide over the spinal cord easily.

As you enter the twist, continue to gauge your movement to avoid any irritation to the spinal cord. (While the brain is insensitive to pain, the outer sheath of the spinal cord is richly supplied with sensory nerve fibers.) Imagine that you are initiating the movement from the level of the spinal cord. If you overpower the spine with the strength of the arm, the result will often be irritation in the spine during the twist and an ache in the back long after your practice is finished.

Once the torso has rotated so the chest is facing the left knee, you can take the “hand lock” by bringing the right arm around the outside of the left shin. Link the fingers or, if possible, hold the left wrist with the right hand. Exhale and draw the hands away from the shoulders, allowing the spine to lengthen strongly upward.

If taking the hand lock compresses the front of the abdomen and collapses the spine, you are moving your skeleton further than the organs can support. Be conscious of using your breath to shape the internal organs. Keep the front of the abdomen open and draw the base of the left rib cage in toward the waist to encourage full spinal extension. Turn the head to look back at the foot of the extended leg (Figure 4). Take a few more breaths and then release. Repeat on the other side.

To clarify the distinction between initiating movement from the inner body and dominating with the outer muscles, you might try the previous exercises again, this time exerting force with the outer body by using the arm as a strong lever. Notice the tone in the muscle tissue when you exert force from the outside, as opposed to the quality when you allow the inner body to give to the movement in its own time. Also notice how the two different ways of initiating movement create different psychological states.

Within each of us is a longing for wholeness. Like the spiraling shape of the twist, our spiritual path must constantly turn back toward the still center within us. The longing to “get somewhere” through yoga is a distortion of our true urge to return back to the undifferentiated, unchanging core from which all life expands.

#8785. From the Brooks Ghost 18 to Adidas Adizero Evo SL, These Are the 10 Best Men’s Running Shoes We Recommend

From road to trail, daily training to racing, these are our top trainers for every kind of runner.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 9, 2026: Our Shoe of the Year and favorite speedwork shoe, the Adidas Adizero Evo SL, is now 20%. We’ve also added its faster cousin, the Adizero Adios Pro 5, to this list. Our testers say it’s even snappier than the Pro 4.

New runners always ask me, “What’s the best running shoe?” But there’s truly not one trainer that outperforms them all. Instead of recommending one single shoe, I consider the runner’s experience level and what they’re training for.

Maybe you signed up for your first 5K or you’re a more experienced runner setting your sights on training for your first marathon. Or maybe you’re trying to get faster or just want a new pair of kicks to start run/walking. From beginner to vet, road to trail, neutral to stability, there’s a shoe out there for everyone.

Men kind of have the upper hand in terms of running shoes because most models are designed for men’s feet by default. Even on unisex racing shoes, runners with smaller ankles (typically women) often need to use special tricks like the heel lock lacing technique to tighten the fit because they were built based on a men’s last with a wider collar.

That doesn’t mean you can zone out when it comes to finding the best fit. We have a handy guide to help you find your approximate size before shopping. There’s also width to consider, as well as intention: Do you want a grippy, durable trail shoe or a lightweight trainer for tempo runs?

Here, we break it down for you by naming our top 10 running shoes for men and provide guidance on what features you should consider.

Looking for a solid daily trainer → Nike Pegasus 42Searching for a mileage monster → New Balance EllipseA new runner → Brooks Ghost 18Adding speedwork → Adidas Adizero Evo SLA run/walker → On Cloudmonster 3An overpronator → Saucony Guide 19Injury-prone → Saucony Triumph 24Needing a wider fit → Hoka Clifton 11Racing a marathon → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5Hitting the trailhead → Altra Experience Wild 3

I’ve chosen to highlight each of these shoes based on feedback from the men on our editorial team, as well as the Runner’s World wear-tester program. We frequently update the lineup to ensure we're giving you the best, most up-to-date recommendations for every type of run—and runner.

Please note: While we’re experts at vetting the best footwear and update these lists often, retailer prices and stock fluctuate constantly. Our recommendations may not always be available in a given size or color. We’ll do our best to update our links to make sure you can get every pick as often as possible.

The Peg is back—and our testing proves it was worth the wait. The newest iteration is snappier and more responsive, thanks to a full-length Air Zoom unit that had one tester say, “the design leans into speed.” The shoe is a major improvement compared to its predecessor, which wasn’t necessarily bad; the Peg 41’s ride was just a little lackluster according to our testers’ feedback.

Nike stepped in to make sure the Pegasus 42 would have more rebound. The last is also modified to accommodate wider feet.

“The Nike Pegasus 42 is a solid and stable everyday trainer. Back in 1990 when I was running cross country in high school, my very first shoe was the Nike Air Pegasus and they have made some excellent changes over the past 35 years,” said tester Steven Blasi.

“The Pegasus 42 is nothing like my Pegasus from my high school days,” he continued. “The shoe is not too hard, not too soft, it is just right. The slight rocker bottom of the shoe made for a nice and smooth transition from heel to forefoot and the [Air Zoom unit] added the extra push.”

With the Ellipse you get an affordable model that packs incredible comfort and bounce. New Balance Senior Global Project Manager Paul Zielinski explained to Runner’s World how the brand set out to capture the communal aspect of our sport in a shoe. Think of the Ellipse as your “running group model,” the shoe’s ride meant to embody the rush of going on a fun run with friends.

The shoe has a retooled version of the brand’s Fresh Foam X; it has new geometry to make it springier. Though the shoe feels slightly bulky—it’s not intended for speedwork—its midsole produces a trampoline-like bounce that energizes your run.

“I like the foam,” said shoe tester and Director of News Andrew Daniels. “Some of the shoes I ran in most recently feel more firm than these, like a gym mat. This isn’t *super* sponge-y, but more in that sweet spot of just-right firm and just-right squishy, where it stays pretty bouncy for most of the run and provides good cushioning on the landings.”

Our men and women testers were split on the Ghost 18. Men liked the shoe’s ride and comfy fit, saying that even though the foam isn’t as responsive as other daily trainers they’ve tested, the Ghost 18 is a reliable shoe for logging easy workouts.

“[The Ghost 18] is well-cushioned, especially in the heel,” said Photo Director John Hamilton. “Really noticed it on a long downhill at the end of a longer run. The foam was supportive and adequate especially for slower paces but lacked a ‘pop’ when picking up the pace.”

Hamilton also noted the toe area felt slightly narrow and that a wider width would remedy this hitch (the shoe is available in wide and extra wide, as well as narrow widths).

On the other end, the air mesh upper was uncomfortable for our women testers, who complained they got hot spots under the big toe area. It’s funny to say an iteration of a shoe works better for men’s feet, but that seems to be the case with our testing—which is why the Ghost 18 made this list as Best Daily Trainer.

“I really like easy cruising, when I lay back on my heel and float,” said Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate. “I think that’s where this shoe works best, and probably why it’s going to work for newer runners and the majority of us who heel strike.”

Dengate said in February 2025 that the Adizero Evo SL was the shoe of the year, and that he’d feast on it if something better came along. What would lead him to make such a bold claim? For starters, the Lightstrike Pro foam in its midsole is the same cushioning Adidas used in its incredibly effective competition-grade marathon shoe, the Adios Pro 4. The Evo SL drops the Pro 4’s carbon-fiber plate in favor of a nylon shank, lending stability in a more affordable way. Because of its best value attributes (you get a heckuva lot for just $150) and dynamic construction, the shoe has been a mainstay on our lists. Dengate is definitely saved from snacking on shoelaces.

The shoe has some minor drawbacks: The tongue tends to go askew mid-run, and the fit was narrow for some of our testers. These were, by the testers’ admissions, pet peeves, though. They all said they’d continue running in the shoe, especially for speedy efforts.

“I like the lightweight feel of these sneakers,” said tester Ahmad Norman. “This helps me glide and turnover my stride at a rapid pace. I can see that training in these sneakers will most certainly increase my tempo and bring down my splits per mile.”

We love the Cloudmonster 3 at any pace, from casual walks to 4:30 strides. Our testers were impressed with the firm—but soft—Helion cushioning that provided a responsive ride for almost any kind of effort.

The shoe has On’s triple-layer CloudTec cushioning, which makes the bounce and support not much of a mystery when you see the system of holes on the shoe’s rocker shape. A Speedboard promotes propulsion and smooth push-off.

“When I slid my foot into these shoes to try on at the pickup I was instantly blown away with the shear joy it was to have these shoes on my feet,” said shoe tester Dave Brattley. “Needless to say there were some high expectations for them to perform just as well during run and they didn’t disappoint! Fit and feel, check, forefoot cushioning that’s soft but you can still feel the road, check, heel cushioning while walking, check, and durability, check! There wasn’t anything that felt off about these shoes.”

The Guide 19 is basically the same—thank goodness!—as its predecessor. It features the brand’s CenterPath technology, which adds a broader base and higher sidewalls to create a more cradled fit that provides support without constriction. Wide-footed testers love how this feature also creates an accommodating fit in the midfoot.

Pwrrun foam provides max-cushioning, making the shoe suitable for long runs and recovery days. The shoe’s rocker profile promotes fast turnover.

“Like its predecessor, this shoe made me feel good before even starting my runs,” said tester Dave Block. “I just love the comfort and feel! The shoe is very soft and slips on easily. I can’t think of any other shoe that feels this great, with the possible exception of the Adidas Pureboost, but that’s going back several years.”

The Triumph 24 is a true triumph for Saucony. The max-cushioned shoe is a mere 8.8 ounces in a men’s size 9. That’s lighter than our favorite daily trainer, the Ghost 18. The shoe’s new IncrediLux foam provides an incredibly soft—but supportive—platform.

The foam also delivers high rebound, resulting in runs that start off slow then gradually go uptempo because of the shoe’s blend of comfort and high energy return.

Testers loved the fit and feel of the trainer. For runner Phil Nicolosi, it was all about the journey and not about the stats on his watch.

“I rated the Saucony Triumph 24 very highly overall because it was one of the most comfortable max-cushioned shoes I have worn,” he said. “The fit was excellent, the upper was comfortable, and the cushioning made it easy on my aging body. It was especially good for scenic, easy runs when I was not worried about pace and just wanted to enjoy being out there.”

The Clifton is the epitome of a Hoka trainer: soft and supportive cushioning; padded, comfy, accommodating upper; rocker geometry that smooths heel-to-toe transitions. Known for its max-cushioned models, Hoka released two Cliftons this year. The Clifton Pro is an amped-up version of the Clifton 11. But in terms of recommending the best men’s shoes, I’m sticking with the original Clifton.

The Clifton 11 is like running with an old friend. The daily trainer’s rep is up there with the Nike Peg and Brooks Ghost for its overall comfort and responsive ride. The shoe has a compression-molded EVA midsole (CMEVA). Even though it’s comparatively not as bouncy as other trainers with superior foams, you still get high-energy return for daily miles and excellent support running long. It’s also a favorite for run/walking.

Hoka Clifton 11 Running Review | Hoka Clifton 11 Walking Review

The shoe worn by the fastest man, Sabastian Sawe, was the Adidas Adios Pro Evo 3. That shoe sold out in record time—at a pretty penny for $500. The next best thing? The Adidas Adios Pro 5, which is about half the price and in stock now.

The Pro 5 features a new carbon form in the shoe’s midsole; in place of rods, which mapped out the pad of your foot like your metatarsals, Adidas introduces a carbon rim. According to the brand, the rim results in 12.5 percent weight savings. Our testers found the new tech even more explosive than the Pro 4. The ride is snappy and delivers an aggressive but stable bounce thanks to the updated Lightstrike Pro foam, which is slightly firmer.

Dengate praised the shoe’s performance during a speed workout—even though he got dropped. “I loved that I could feel the foam compress and load up with each footstrike, yet feel bouncy and responsive at toe-off,” he said. “These shoes wanted more than my legs could give.”

The Experience Wild 3 has supportive cushioning without limiting ground feel, 3.5mm lugs that bite into loose terrain, and a comfortable, accommodating fit that allows you to splay your toes when hitting the trail.

With a 4mm drop, it’s a good option for runners not ready to commit to zero-drop but who still want to dabble in low-drop. The upper has a protective toe sweep and gaiter attachments.

“[The Experience Wild 3] takes the shoe to the next level with a redesigned upper that fits more generously but doesn’t make you feel like you are swimming around, plusher cushioning that absorbs firmer ground yet remains stable, and a lug pattern on the MaxTrac outsole that I felt was superior to each of the previous models in terms of grip,” said tester John Mikovits.

The shoe is also available with a Vibram Megagrip outsole.

Fit and comfort go hand-in-hand. You don’t want to constantly think of how loose or tight your shoes feel as you run. We recommend looking for a thumbnail’s width of toe room between the tip of your longest toe and the nose of the shoe, which leaves space for your feet to swell as you run.

Generally speaking, your running shoe should be a half size up compared to your regular street shoes. When in doubt, I generally recommend going in for a fitting and getting expert help so you're sure you find your perfect size.

Be mindful of heel rubbing and slipping. You can use the heel lock lacing technique for a snugger fit around the collar. Some runners have a high instep as well. If you feel pressure in the lacing area, you may need a shoe with a wider width.

It’s normal to have some pronation as you run. If your foot rolls excessively inward, however, you may be susceptible to knee and lower back injuries. See a specialist, like a podiatrist or physical therapist, for a gait evaluation. Special insoles and shoes with medial posts can help severe overpronators with erratic foot rolling.

If you have mild pronation or late-onset pronation, some stability shoes have holistic features, like guide rails, that act as subtle bumpers to help you when your form gets sloppy.

We recommend the Brooks Ghost 18 for beginner runners because it provides Goldilocks cushioning: not too soft, nor too hard. It’s a great starting point to see if you sway firm and lightweight or soft and max-cushioned.

Runners prefer lightweight shoes with a thinner midsole for faster efforts. These past years, however, have proven you don’t have to sacrifice stack height for speed thanks to the arrival of super foams. Still, some runners may prefer a simpler, more grounded lightweight racing flat for track workouts or hard tempos.

Max-cushioned trainers are great for long runs and recovery runs postrace, when you’re gradually adding miles again after taking time off from running.

Why should I pay more than $200 for a pair of running shoes?

Top-of-the-line running shoes made for competition feature premium materials, which generally force their prices well over the $200 line. Super foams enhance the running experience; paired with a carbon-fiber plate, this combination can improve your running economy.

These shoes are an investment and a novelty. Not everyone will experience a “4 percent” improvement. And even though super shoes eight years later are made of more durable materials (the recommended usage used to be 100 miles per pair), shelf life is still dependent on the wearer and their wear pattern.

You can also find top quality shoes for a lesser price. Training shoes, like the Saucony Endorphin Speed 6, are constructed with premium foams and have a much lower price tag than their carbon-fiber counterparts.

Can a running shoe actually make me faster?

When Nike released the original Vaporfly in 2017, many runners misinterpreted the brand's “4 percent” claim to mean running 4 percent faster, rather than improving energy efficiency. The combination of responsive super foam with a carbon-fiber plate to work as a stabilizer (the plate actually works in tandem with the foam and isn’t the root cause for propulsion) helps the wearer run more efficiently, using less oxygen and less energy to maintain their speed.

Regardless of what a brand claims, though, the only universal truth about a shoe’s impact on running performance is that no two runners will see the same benefits. A shoe is a tool: It can help you train to become stronger and improve your stride. Lightweight shoes with responsive foams can make you feel swifter and deliver more rebound, but you are the one getting faster.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#8783. The Best Heart Rate Monitors Give You the Most Accurate Training Data

We tested the best heart rate monitors so you can focus on the miles, not the math.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Tracking your heart rate with a heart rate monitor (HRM) during your runs is one of the most powerful ways to optimize your training, whether you’re a dedicated marathoner, power triathlete, or just aiming to move more intentionally. As a runner, I understand that my heart rate is important, but I don’t necessarily understand using it as a training device. That’s why I reached out to an expert to find out why it’s important and how to use that data.

As exercise physiologist and run coach Alyssa Lombardi tells Runner’s World, “Monitoring your heart rate while training can be a great tool to help you understand how hard your body is working. It’s important for a balanced training program to have lots of easy recovery days where your heart rate is low, balanced by some harder intensity workouts where your heart rate is high.” Understanding and utilizing heart-rate zones—ranging from zone 1 (very light) to zone 5 (maximum effort)—can help you tailor your training for performance, endurance, and recovery.

While zone 2 running gets loads of buzz as the golden ticket for endurance building and recovery, Lombardi emphasizes that “all zones have their place in a training program.” She also notes an important caveat: “As an exercise physiologist I can understand the benefits of heart rate training but when I am coaching my athletes I do not have them follow heart rate based training to a T because your heart rate can vary so much day to day.” Lombardi lists how factors like heat, hydration, location, and medications can change your heart rate. “It is a great tool to have but I never have my athletes follow that 100 percent.”

This nuanced approach is critical—HRMs are invaluable tools, but their data should be viewed in context. Each athlete responds differently, and some exceptionally fit runners may see higher heart rates at lower intensity simply because their bodies have adapted to efficiently sustain greater workloads.

As a side note, these are largely HSA/FSA eligible, so you might not be out-of-pocket for the cost. Just check your eligibility, and keep those receipts.

Alyssa Lombardi is a certified personal trainer, run coach, and clinical exercise physiologist with more than six years of experience. A former collegiate runner with a master’s in exercise science, she coaches athletes of all levels through her business, Run Fit With Me. Lombardi emphasizes individualized training, injury prevention, and strength work, blending evidence-based science with real-world experience to help runners get faster, stay healthy, and achieve their goals.

The Polar H10 stands out as the best overall heart rate monitor for its unmatched accuracy and comfort. Its ECG technology delivers precise data, making it a favorite among serious athletes. The soft, non-slip strap comes in multiple sizes, but women should note it can be a tricky fit with some supportive sports bras—though it works comfortably under lower-line running tank bras. Men with chest hair have mentioned a slight pulling sensation, but most find it secure once adjusted. With long battery life, waterproofing up to 30 meters, dual Bluetooth connectivity, and onboard memory, it’s a reliable companion for any training style.

The Powr Labs Chest Heart Rate Monitor offers solid performance for a fraction of the price of premium brands, making it a great budget-friendly option. I found the strap to be comfortable and adjustable, though the sensor is a bit bulky. Its dual ANT+ and Bluetooth connectivity worked seamlessly with my Garmin and smartphone apps.

While it’s water-resistant, I’d avoid prolonged swimming sessions. It tracks heart rate reliably across different workouts, from running to CrossFit. The strap fits well on me, but it might feel a bit tight or loose for some depending on body shape. Overall, it’s a dependable, no-frills monitor that gets the job done without breaking the bank, especially if this is your first foray into HR training.

If you have a Forerunner 570 or above, you’ll know that some of the more advanced metrics like cadence and step speed loss require a heart rate monitor for measurement. This HRM is not only the best for that application but also one of the best we tested—period. It’s unbelievably comfy, it’s incredibly accurate, and it syncs seamlessly with whatever Garmin watch you use, and it’s not limited to only Garmin devices. You love your Apple Watch? Fab. Use it. You don’t run with a watch? First of all, how dare you. Second of all, it still works. You just need to link it to your phone instead. (You’re a rebel. I don’t get it, but I appreciate it.)

I do wish that it came in more and extended sizes. And honestly, if you’re stacked through the lats and pecs, it might not work, which is unfortunately pretty much true for the majority of chest straps. But for the majority of runners, this is an economical, comfortable, feature-packed choice that gets you into Garmin’s system. Welcome to the cult.

The Coros Heart Rate Monitor is my favorite pick when I want accurate tracking without the chest strap drama. The soft, stretchy fabric band hugs my upper arm comfortably—no digging, no slipping—and works well for a wide range of arm sizes. I barely feel it on long runs, and it never tangles with my tops. The optical sensor stays steady most of the time, though it can lag a bit on sudden sprints. It’s a bit more laggy than other HRMs I tested, by a few seconds. This is not a unique problem to Coros, but it is more noticeable here.

Battery life is solid at up to 38 hours, and Bluetooth syncing is quick, but the connection range isn’t amazing—you’ll want to keep your watch or phone fairly close. I’ve also noticed it can get a little itchy once I start sweating hard, so a quick postrun rinse is a must. Still, for comfort, simplicity, and ditching the chest strap, it’s a win in my book.

The Whoop Peak is a heckuva fun wearable device for deep health and fitness insights—tracking not just your heart rate, but also recovery, sleep quality, strain, and more. I love how all that data comes together to show me exactly when to push harder and when to rest. I am notorious for doing all the things, all at once, like training for a marathon while also working on a deadline for my book and keeping my demanding day job. This is great for my AuDHD brain, but can be hard on my body. The Whoop dials into that and lets me know I’ve been going too hard and my recovery metrics are showing that. The only real trade-off with this wearable? You have to look at your phone for every stat, since the band has no face or display.

And while you do pay for a monthly membership to access the full suite of features, the first year is included, which makes it easier to justify. It doesn’t warn you as often as the Oura ring or a Garmin device about your habits, but features a lighter touch in the “you’re overdoing it” shame department.

The Garmin HRM-Fit has totally changed how I think about heart rate straps. Instead of wrapping around my chest like the usual band (and fighting with my sports bra every run), it clips right onto the underband of a medium- or high-support bra. No chafing, no slipping—just accurate tracking that feels almost invisible once I get going.

It did take a minute to learn how to get the clips sitting just right, but now it’s second nature. My heart rate data is spot-on, and I love that it pairs instantly with my Garmin watch and other devices via Bluetooth or ANT+. The chunky clips do show under tight tops, so it’s not exactly stealthy, but the yearlong battery life makes up for it. For me, it’s comfort, accuracy, and freedom—all in one.

I am a big fan of the upgrades on the Oura Ring 5. First of all, it’s a lot slimmer and lighter than previous models, and it also doesn’t scratch as easily. On top of that, the battery life is much improved. But what really matters is what the ring does.

It’s an accurate HRM that picks up activities easily, sometimes too easily, as it can occasionally register things like vacuuming as “dancing” or cleaning the bathroom as “HIIT.” Though that might speak more to the vigor with which I scrub the bathroom than any mistake of the ring itself.

When I’m on my run, it tracks my heart rate, oxygen, and effort and gives me insights on where I can improve and what I can do to achieve that, and it’s easy to understand and well thought out. But what I really love is how it looks at my cycle, and helps me understand how that might be affecting my workouts. As it turns out, perimenopause is messing with my life hard-core, and now my previously unpredictable cycle has become even more unpredictable, and it’s making my runs around my period so much worse.

But there’s help in the app for that, as well. In the app, you can connect with health practitioners or link to your own healthcare provider, upload your labs, food diary, and more, and get advice based on your current goals and situation. I recently linked to my primary care doctor and my hematologist to determine just how my cycle, training, diet, and anemia were affecting each other, and we came up with a plan for treatment. To the infusion clinic I go! Before I had this ability, the process was a lot longer and a much bigger pain in the butt. Now, my doctors and I can make concrete plans far more easily, and it’s been a big blessing.

Accuracy is paramount for heart rate monitors. A reliable HRM provides consistent, precise heart rate readings during various activities, from cardio to strength training. Inaccurate readings can undermine workout effectiveness and hinder fitness progress, making you wonder if your heart is even trying.

When it comes to heart rate tracking, it’s all about what feels right for you, especially when you’re really pushing it. Chest straps give you accurate readings but can be a bit annoying, while wrist monitors and rings are convenient but might glitch out during intense workouts. So, the real MVP here is whatever you’ll actually wear and trust for your grind—try ’em both if you can.

Say goodbye to connection woes. Thanks to Bluetooth and ANT+, gadgets play nice with all your beloved external devices and go-to fitness apps. Some even have the ability to send the readings right to your doctor.

No one likes a dead heart rate monitor in the middle of a workout, so think about how often you’ll need to swap out those batteries. Make sure you have a good stash of fresh ones on hand, or consider rechargeable options to keep the fun going. That way, your entertainment won’t be interrupted by a sudden power outage.

A durable HRM needs to keep up with your lifestyle, whether you’re breaking a sweat or just enjoying a brisk walk. Chest bands are generally very durable, while smartwatches and wristbands offer good longevity but may be a bit more precious, and smart health tracking rings are designed for continuous wear and can withstand daily activities but may scratch.

Running dynamics, on-device memory, and water resistance can enhance utility for diverse athletes. Additionally, some advanced watches and rings offer features like period and ovulation prediction, providing valuable health insights for users. These capabilities make them more than just fitness trackers, transforming them into comprehensive personal health companions.

These can get pricey. Select a monitor that fits your budget and needs, and don’t forget that some, like the Whoop and Oura ring, have additional membership fees.

Many standard heart rate monitors—especially chest straps and armbands—pose real and annoying challenges for size inclusivity. Limited strap size ranges often make them too small for bigger runners and too large or bulky for petite athletes, affecting comfort, fit, and even accuracy.

For women with large breasts who require more supportive bras, chest straps can be particularly tricky. Supportive or high-compression bras may push the strap down, create pressure points, or cause shifting, which can lead to discomfort, chafing, or inconsistent readings. When shopping for a heart rate monitor, it’s important to consider not only strap length and adjustability but also how well the design works with your body type and workout apparel to ensure both comfort and reliable data.

How accurate are wrist-based HRMs compared to chest straps?Wrist-based optical sensors are good these days—accurate enough for most people—but chest straps still win during activities with sudden heart rate spikes or lots of wrist movement.

Do I need a subscription for my HRM?Most HRMs don’t require one, but some, like Whoop or Oura, do charge a monthly membership for access to their full analytics and insights. That subscription cost is worth factoring into your budget.

Can heart rate monitors detect health issues?HRMs aren’t medical devices, but trends in your heart rate, recovery, or heart rhythm can signal changes worth discussing with your healthcare provider. Some devices, like the Apple Watch, even have FDA-cleared ECG apps to record heart rhythm data.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.
