#8781. I Got Shingles Training for a Marathon. I’m Not the Only One.

Shingles typically appears as a band of blistering, painful rash on one side of the body. (Photo: Getty Images)

I had just finished the last hard training run of my marathon build, 19 miles with 15 at race pace. I nailed it, but couldn’t help thinking it felt harder than it should have.

“It’s just nerves,” I told myself. “You’ll have two weeks to taper, and you’ll be ready to run that BQ (Boston Marathon Qualifying time) on race day.”

The next day, I felt exhausted, and my ribs were sore and tender to the touch. I started to wonder if I’d pulled a muscle in my rib cage while breathing heavily during my training run. I, of course, turned to Google. “Ribs sore from running.” “Ribs hurt after running.” Most of the posts advised that I’d feel better in a day.

But I didn’t feel better the next day. Instead, I noticed a small pink mark on my stomach, and now my ribs felt both sore and tingly. My Google searches grew more alarming: I could have shingles.

I scheduled an appointment for that same day, and my doctor confirmed it. She took one look at me and said, “I’m so sorry, you have shingles.”

Shingles is a painful viral infection that looks like a terrible rash and usually involves nerve pain that can last for months. The virus comes from dormant chickenpox in your body that can reappear when you’re stressed.

My doctor asked about stressors in my life. “I haven’t really been that stressed,” I promised, saying my family life and my career were extremely smooth. “But I have been training for a marathon,” I said.

“That could do it,” she told me. “Your body is clearly telling you that you were pushing too hard.”

I’m 43, younger than the typical shingles patient, but I’m part of an unfortunate trend. Shingles cases are on the rise and the biggest increase is among people in their 30s and 40s. One study found overall shingles cases nearly doubled between 2005 and 2021. Another found cases in Americans under 50 quadrupled from the late 1940s to 2000, and are still going up, according to data from the CDC.

A big reason for the increase among millennials is that we fall into a gap: 50 and up, and you can get the shingles vaccine; 30 and under, and you’ve had the chickenpox vaccine, which will make getting shingles way less likely.

That age range is also most common among marathoners, so my big question was whether running, especially hard training, can give you shingles. Unfortunately, that specific question hasn’t been extensively studied, so there’s no clear-cut answer. But doctors are drawing correlations between heavy training and whether it decreases the body’s immunity overall.

There’s research that shows immunity dips after heavy training, says David Nieman, DrPH, FACSM, director of the Human Performance Laboratory at Appalachian State University. He pointed to a study involving mice and the herpes virus.

“When you infected the mice and then forced them to run to exhaustion, there was a higher mortality rate in those mice than mice that just did moderate activity and rested,” he says. “Moderate activity actually helped a little bit, but by far the really bad response was in the mice that ran to exhaustion.”

In another study, researchers gave horses the flu and then ran them really hard. Those horses developed a longer-lasting, more intense bout of the flu compared to the horses who were infected but didn’t run hard, he said.

But Nieman and other researchers agree that moderate exercise can actually boost your immunity. James Turner, a professor at the Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation Sciences school at the University of Birmingham, says it’s far more common that inadequate sleep, diet and psychological stress suppress immunity than exercise, even really hard training.

“Research on both prolonged exercise and marathon running shows that antibody responses are not suppressed and might actually be higher,” he says.

Meanwhile, Dr. William Schaffner, MD, a professor of infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health who’s an expert in shingles, says it’s too soon to say definitely that lots of stress leads to the virus. He points out there’s no evidence that soldiers in combat or police and firefighters have an increased risk of shingles.

“When people get a shingles episode, there is a tendency to look back in their lives to see if there might be some sort of inciting event or stressful event and there’s a tendency to link the two,” he says. “But the question is, is that just coincidence because there’s a lot of stress in life, or was it a causal relationship? I think we’ll still have to say that hasn’t been definitively settled.”

Instead, for Schaffner, the likeliest explanation for the increase in shingles is because the chickenpox vaccine is decreasing our exposure to chickenpox. We used to all get chickenpox as children, and so the virus was more common in the wild. That gave our immune systems a boost. Now that there’s a vaccine, that isn’t happening, which means we may be more likely to get shingles, he said.

Whether my running caused my shingles or not, as soon as I had my diagnosis, my next questions were about my marathon. My doctor said my symptoms would likely peak in four days to a week, and so it still seemed possible I would be ready for race day. I rushed out to get a seven-day course of Valtrex—if you start an antiviral treatment quickly enough, it can stop the spread of the shingles rash.

But as the week passed and the rash grew along my rib cage to my back, it only continued to feel worse. I was achy everywhere, and my ribs felt like they were constantly being stabbed with tiny needles. A week later, I called it and canceled my marathon plans, harboring a hope that within a few weeks I would be better and could rebound to run my BQ.

What I did next probably hurt my cause rather than helped it. As soon as I felt a bit better, I would go out and do a race-pace run, which would give me a painful setback that lasted for several days. This likely was making my bout with the virus longer, Nieman says.

He reminded me of the mice who were running to exhaustion and not getting well. The mice really needed to keep it low-key to get an immune boost, not drain.

“If they did 30 minutes of something like a brisk walk equivalent, that would help a little bit,” he says.

My conversation with him sounded like a negotiation.

“I’m mostly feeling better, but I still sometimes have sensations in my ribs, so do I still need to take it easy?” I asked.

“I have a lot of empathy. I know you don’t want to hear it,” he said gently. Nieman has run 58 marathons himself, so he knows the feeling. “You don’t want anybody telling you not to run, but this is where you’ve got to be really, really careful and just bide your time and slowly get back into it once you feel better.”

His advice to runners: listen to your body and don’t push yourself. That’s not an easy metric for marathoners who are used to pushing beyond what feels comfortable, but Nieman says exhaustion can exacerbate the nerve pain and make it all last much longer.

Other things to keep in mind: it’s possible that sunburns can impede your immune system, so cover up once you’re back out and running, says Jennifer Moffat, a SUNY microbiology and immunology professor and expert on chickenpox and shingles.

And, Moffat says, while you still have a rash, you’re contagious and can spread the virus to others through contact. If you’re at the gym or anywhere you might touch other people, you should have the rash fully covered.

She also advises keeping an eye on the other stresses around marathons, like not eating enough, not sleeping enough, and the mental stress around races.

“The anticipation, logistics, travel hassles, changes in environment and food, rivalries with other competitors, jet lag, time away from family, the cost can become overwhelming,” she says. “Getting to the starting line of a marathon is much more than showing up with your shoes tied.”

In fact, she says, it’s common for people to come down with other viral infections right before a race (the dreaded taper cold).

As for me, two months after my rash first appeared, I finally truly threw in the towel. I couldn’t keep up any kind of marathon training without making myself feel worse, so I switched to low-effort maintenance running and decided my BQ would have to come next year.

#8780. Veterans Who Turned to Yoga Are Now Teaching It—And Not Always in the Places You’d Expect

Veterans yoga has been in existence for decades, with several organizations providing free classes. But what has been changing is the number of veterans teaching yoga, both to their peers and the general public. Writer “Chez” Chesak explores how his former platoonmates and other former military personnel are introducing others to the practice.

When I was deployed to Iraq with the U.S. Army in 2005, me and the rest of my platoon were constantly jumping in and out of Humvees, ascending uneven stairs in buildings, climbing ladders in guard towers, and generally finding ourselves in constant motion—all with more than 80 pounds of armor, ammo, night vision goggles, and other combat load sitting on our shoulders. And then there was the tremendous and relentless emotional and psychological stress. Needless to say, we were all very wired and very, very tight.

One proactive and thoughtful soldier in our platoon, Jake Smith, suggested that yoga could probably help and offered to download some instructions and lead us through a class. For some reason—quite possibly to stay out of sight from other soldiers, who would have likely ridiculed us—we thought it best to climb onto the roof of our building in Kirkuk for an ad hoc yoga session. Jake, who was definitely not a certified instructor but certainly did his best, led us through various poses and we attempted to follow along.

Somewhere in between making shapes with my body and concentrating on my breath, it registered that there were dozens of buildings in plain view of our patrol base. And if we could see the surrounding buildings, anyone in those buildings could see us. Realizing that we could be in the sights of a sniper, we quickly wrapped up class and made our way back inside.

For most of us, it was our first attempt at yoga. Despite the fact the class was well-intentioned and received well, none of us continued practicing during our time overseas. Instead, we succumbed to more shoulder pain and mental duress.

But in the years since, some in my platoon—as well as active military personnel and veterans everywhere—have been getting past our initial biases against such a “hippy” activity and turning to yoga for an array of reasons, including support with lingering physical and mental health challenges. I’ve heard the quote “Yoga saved my life,” from numerous military veterans who expressed the sentiment with zero embellishment, exaggeration, or hyperbole.

With nearly 16 million veterans in the U.S., there are more who could benefit from yoga. A survey of 300,000 veterans and service members registered with the Wounded Warrior Project found that more than half of respondents struggled to manage their pain, with 95 percent experiencing pain in the previous three months and 76 percent acknowledging that pain interfered with their ability to enjoy life. Additionally, more than 50 percent experienced anxiety symptoms in the previous two weeks.

Many of the veterans who proselytize about yoga know firsthand its role in supporting individuals through the repercussions of surviving combat zones. Some proceed to take yoga teacher training and introduce others to the practice, sharing it every conceivable style and practice space, including studios, gyms, and corporate offices. And among them are also those helping fellow soldiers and veterans explore how yoga might help them navigate the complexities of PTSD.

Mike Cappel used to hate yoga. He served 12 years in Military Intelligence in the Army Reserve and three years as a Combat Engineer in the National Guard and readily admits his past loathing for the practice.

Thanks to doctor’s orders, he tried yoga, fell in love with it, and then took a summer class at the University of Cincinnati (U.C.). Cappel now teaches yoga to the Reserve Officers Training Corps cadets there, beginning with cadets who participated in his yoga warm-ups before the Army Combat Fitness Test (ACFT) swearing that they scored higher thanks to the practice.

“They all say they love it now,” says Cappel. “And I can see that they really do. We’ll have a whole battalion of people out there in the stadium first thing in the morning, all doing yoga.” The officers that run the program eventually decided to try his classes as well,and these days everyone does yoga together before taking the ACFT.

His yoga instruction isn’t limited to students in uniform. Cappel also teaches at the offices of corporate clients, local independent yoga studios, and chain gyms, and leads a total of 16 classes a week.

In contrast to exposing those new to the military to yoga, Chris Smith brings it to those who have come back from their tours of duty and struggle to reacclimate to everyday life. After serving as an Engineer in the Army for eight years and being deployed three times, including during the 2003 Iraq invasion, Chris separated from the military and from his wife. He was unhoused and struggling with substance abuse when he was committed to an involuntary five-day psychiatric hold at a hospital.

Eventually, Chris landed in a rental assistance program through Veteran Affairs (VA), used the GI Bill to get a degree from Marywood University, and then started a veteran resource center. In researching benefits, he learned about Warrior Strong, which provides free wellness services, including yoga, to veterans across 33 states.

Chris explains that after taking his first yoga class, he was hooked. He soon signed up for training to become an instructor. He and other Warrior Strong instructors currently deliver nearly 100 classes spanning yoga, fitness, meditation, and breathwork to veterans each month. The classes are conducted online as well as in-studio at the Scranton, Pennsylvania, location as well regional VA medical centers. He also volunteers his teaching time to a weekly breathwork class for the depression group at a local veterans center and a monthly meditation class at the drug and alcohol unit at a VA Medical Center.

“Yoga is what’s really helping me manage my PTSD symptoms,” says Chris. “It’s helped me reconnect with people because for a very long time I was isolating myself a lot. I credit it with helping me continue the journey that I started nine years ago.”

Other veterans take elements of how yoga best supports them and share it with a more generalized student population. Jessica Armendariz spent 21 years in the U.S. Army, serving in the Airborne, completing all four levels of the Amy’s Combatives hand-to-hand combat training, and deploying to Afghanistan. When she retired, her body was experiencing severe physical wear, joint pain, and elevated cortisol levels. She eventually found that practicing rigorous vinyasa yoga helped alleviate chronic pain and quiet her racing mind.

Armendariz currently teaches studio classes at Hot Asana in Southern Pines, North Carolina, and tries to share the same benefits with others. “I am trying to challenge you physically,” says Armendariz. “That’s not to say that the rest of the yoga goes out the window. Of course we do breathing, we do centering, and all those critical things, but for me, for it to work to feel authentic to me as a teacher, there has to be that challenge.” She also has training in yoga nidra as well as yin and restorative yoga.

Sometimes the adaptability of yoga and its built-in community become as much a part of the yoga experience as the poses. After Jeremy McMullen left the Navy, he became severely sedentary. That’s when his wife gifted him a yoga lesson. The retired Chief Petty Officer instantly found that it benefited his sleep as well as his physical and mental health. Now a yoga instructor, McMullen teaches in a studio, performs yoga on mountain passes during long-distance hikes, has led online classes, and teaches “beer yoga” at breweries, where the participants indulge in a beer or two together afterward.

McMullen sees a correlation between his role in the Navy and his role as an instructor. “The chiefs at work [in the Navy] are always trying to teach sailors the right way to do everything. I do the same thing as a yoga teacher, making sure to teach you your left and your right and your breathing and your mindfulness.”

Military veterans are no strangers to working in unexpected and remote places. Jared McKenzie, a medic in my platoon when we deployed, currently teaches yoga at studios, so it wasn’t entirely a surprise when he was inspired, during a recent multi-day whitewater rafting trip, to lead others through early morning stretches along the shore. He’ll be resuming his beach yoga classes on the outfitter’s 2027 River Soul Journeys whitewater rafting and yoga trip in Idaho.

McKenzie is looking forward to teaching yoga within the solitude and serenity of Idaho’s river canyons. “I love the juxtaposition of this trip where everyone will be blasting whitewater through the day and then slowing down in the evenings with riverside yoga and breathwork,” he says.

There are surely more vets out there who are just now trying a class and starting their own experience with yoga journey. Those who take the next step and become instructors can deploy out to studios and VA facilities, teach online, and maybe even lead a class in a river canyon or other backcountry location. And I choose to believe that none of them will be so foolish as to attempt a class on a rooftop in a combat zone.

Veterans interested in trying yoga will find free resources for veterans-focused, in-person and online classes and teacher trainings through the VA’s Whole Health program and various organizations, including Wounded Warrior Project, Veterans Yoga Project, and VEToga.

#8779. Inspired by Fall Marathon Season? Here’s What You Need to Do to Prepare for 26.2

Follow these nine coach-approved training tips now for a strong finish later.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The spirit of the fall marathon is undeniably contagious: the roaring crowds, the crisp autumn air, and massive community energy. If you spectated this year, watching the hundreds (if not thousands) of runners race toward the finish line might have you yearning to lace up your shoes and hit the starting line next season. But before you jump into training, hit pause and make sure you’re prepared for success.

“Training to run a marathon will revolutionize your life, but it will also test you in brand-new ways,” says Susie Crossland-Dwyer, an avid marathoner and ultramarathoner, coach, and founder of studio s in Cincinnati. “A lot goes into a healthy, successful training season and what you do leading up to it.”

Here are nine tips that coaches want every marathoner to know to get to race day healthy, strong, and fast!

You’re about to set out on four-plus months of intense weekly mileage. That’s really tough on your body. To sidestep an overuse injury, having a steady foundation is crucial. A review of research on runners’ injuries published in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that the injury incidence rate among runners is 40.2 percent, and overuse from ramping up mileage or intensity too quickly causes more than 70 percent of the injuries.

“As you begin your marathon season, start with base building and don’t just jump right into doing all the miles and all the speed workouts,” advises Crossland-Dwyer, who recommends spending at least three months gradually working up to 20 to 25 miles per week before starting an official marathon training program.

“Strength training, specifically your core and hips, is the most effective way to prevent injuries,” says Jeff Gaudette, owner and head coach at RunnersConnect. “As you ramp up your mileage for the marathon, this will be essential to you staying healthy through the training segment.”

Studies have found that strength training can also boost your performance by improving your running economy. You don’t need a certain base of strength before starting your training plan, he says, but you should include two to three weight workouts each week.

Along with weight training, “try plyometrics to get your body used to absorbing impact, single-leg exercises to prevent muscle imbalances, and mobility drills to keep your range of motion and joints healthy,” advises Meg Takacs, NASM-CPT, a run coach and founder of the Movement & Miles app.

Carb-loading before race day is what most novice runners are familiar with when starting on their marathon-training journey, but it’s only one aspect of your diet that’s important.

“Nutrition is key for successful training and a successful race—from carbs to water, electrolytes, and salt capsules,” says Takacs. “The goal is to stay ahead of any deficits before they happen because once you’re in a hydration or nutritional deficit, it’s almost impossible to come back.”

Buy water bottles to carry with you on long runs (sip water or a sports drink every 10 to 15 minutes), plus gels or gummies to nibble on every 30 minutes to stay fueled and strong through your long runs ahead.

We’re not talking about the race itself—though, yes, you’re going to be on your feet for a long time for that, too. But it’s important to know the kind of time commitment you’re going to be looking at for the next 16 or so weeks leading up to race day.

You’ll be devoting a couple hours, at least, likely every Saturday or Sunday morning to a long run, plus your other weekly runs. But also, says Crossland-Dwyer, “Training for a marathon isn’t all about running. In fact, a big portion of your weekly training hours should be spent preparing, with prehab exercises and prerun activations, doing strength-training, and recovering with mobility work, adequate rest and refueling, and extras like compression and cold therapy.”

Yes, destination races are popular, and if you’re pretty sure this whole marathon thing is going to be a one-and-done experience for you, you might as well pick an epic course. But don’t ignore races in your backyard.

“It’s so fun to see your city streets opened up for you,” says Erin Beck, vice president of innovation, product, and experience at Xponential Fitness, who’s run 21 marathons. “Seeing your city from a different vantage point than usual can keep your mind off of the treachery of 26.2 miles.”

Yes, you have several months until race day. But don’t wait to find your favorite clothing and shoes. “Purchase the gear you’ll need now, including shoes for training, the shoes you’ll race in, your potential race kit, and options for different weather conditions,” Gaudette says. “That way, you can test everything out during a few training runs to ensure it’s comfortable.”

Don’t forget about accessories: Having the right details for you, from the fuel belt that bounces the least on your hips to the socks that help you sidestep blisters, will make training all the more comfortable.

If you’re not sure where to start, check out a local running store or online forums for recs from knowledgeable contributors.

Runners joke about bloody nipples for a reason. Rubbed-raw skin there—or your inner thighs or armpit or your upper arm where it shifts against your shirt or sports bra—is inevitable at some point (or several) during marathon training.

Blisters from ill-fitting shoes or the wrong socks could be in your near future too. “Unfortunately, the only way to really know what clothing will contribute to this to test it out, which is why it’s good to have everything you might wear early,” says Gaudette.

In the meantime, buy an anti-chafing stick or cream now and lube up before every long run ahead to protect your skin and slash the chances that you’ll be in a lot of pain later.

All the anticipation of gearing up for your race will likely be mixed with nervousness, too. Remind yourself that you can do this because so many people like you have done the same.

“You don’t have to be Eliud Kipchoge to run a race—and you don’t have to know who that is to run a race, either!” says Beck. “The only thing you have to be in order to be a marathoner is bold enough to try one.”

Every successful marathoner has a training plan to follow. So before you dive into marathon training, you’ll want to find a plan that spans at least 16 weeks and fits your fitness level and your goals.

Do you just want to finish? Are you looking to break three, four, or five hours? Can you meet the weekly mileage in week one of the plan? Think about these questions and find the plan that works to guide you to the starting line and finish line feeling strong.

#8777. Is Your Cycling Computer Lying to You?

Your power meter might be working perfectly, but that doesn’t mean your cycling computer records data accurately. Here’s why you should care and how you can check.

Spend enough time comparing power meters, and you’ll quickly learn that they don’t always agree. Put a power meter on your crank and another on your pedals, and the numbers may not match exactly. That can be frustrating when you’re trying to figure out which one is right, but for most riders, a small, consistent difference isn’t necessarily a problem.

If you use a power meter for training, what matters most is that the numbers you’re seeing today are comparable to the ones you saw last week or last month. Whether your threshold is actually 250 watts or 255 watts matters less than knowing that an interval at that power represents the same effort from one ride to the next.

But what if your power meter isn’t the only thing affecting those numbers? What if the bike computer recording your ride is changing the data before you ever upload it to Strava or TrainingPeaks?

I recently noticed something odd while testing a cycling computer. At first, I was doing this to compare GPS track accuracy, but since I was testing, I also paired all the devices to my heart rate strap and Quarq power meter. When I compared the ride files afterward, what stood out was that their power numbers didn’t match. Initially, the differences were small enough. But when I looked more closely, I noticed it immediately. Every time I stopped pedaling, one computer still recorded power.

Before I get into what the heck sticky watts are, I should say I first learned about the issue in 2025 when I saw a video from Shane Miller, who goes by GPLama on YouTube. The video is called “Power Meter Data Recording: The Wild West?”, and it’s worth watching. Shane was the first person I saw digging into this particular recording issue with cycling computers.

So what the heck is it? Sticky watts happen when a cycling computer keeps recording a power value for a few seconds after you’ve stopped pedaling. Instead of dropping to zero, the last power number gets “stuck” in your ride file until the computer finally catches up.

Let’s say you’re riding along at 250 watts and stop pedaling as you approach a corner. Your computer might continue recording 250 watts for a few seconds while you’re coasting. On a graph, that can look like a flat line extending beyond the point where the power should have dropped.

A few seconds might not sound like much, but think about how often you stop pedaling on a typical ride. Every corner, descent, stop sign, or moment spent coasting in the group is another opportunity for those extra watts to show up in your file. And if you stop pedaling after a hard effort, the computer could be holding a much higher number than 250 watts, which can skew your data.

It’s also worth distinguishing this from the setting on some computers that lets you exclude zeroes when calculating average power. That setting changes how an average is calculated. Sticky watts affect the power values recorded in the ride file itself, so those extra values can still be there when you upload the ride for analysis.

On one ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Garmin Edge 850 and an Edge 1060. The two Garmins recorded almost identical power numbers, but the DURA 2 consistently came out higher. When I looked more closely at the files, I found repeated instances where the COROS continued recording the last power value after both Garmins had dropped to zero.

The difference was especially noticeable during a series of short, hard efforts. After one effort, the DURA 2 recorded 565 watts for four seconds while both Garmins recorded zero. After another, it held 656 watts for three seconds. Across a roughly three-minute section containing several of these efforts, the Garmins averaged about 260 watts, while the COROS recorded nearly 307 watts.

Those short efforts make the issue easy to see, but the difference showed up across the ride, too. In the roughly 98 minutes of matched power data I compared, the DURA 2 averaged about 186 watts, while both Garmins averaged about 179 watts.

On a second ride, I compared the DURA 2 with a Hammerhead Karoo, Wahoo ELEMNT ACE, and Garmin Edge 850. Again, the COROS recorded higher power through a section with several hard efforts followed by coasting. The Garmin recorded lower numbers than the Karoo and Wahoo in that section, which reminds us that differences can go both ways when computers record the same power meter.

I was honestly surprised to see this on the DURA 2. The original DURA had similar issues early on, but its power recording improved with subsequent updates, and it performed well in GPLama’s 2025 video presenting the issue. I don’t want to turn this into a story about picking on COROS. The company has a good history of updating and improving its products, and I expect it can address this issue on the DURA 2 as well. For now, these files show why it’s worth paying attention to what your cycling computer records, even when you trust your power meter.

If you mostly ride for fun and don’t pay much attention to your power data afterward, a few extra watts in your ride file probably won’t change your life. But if you use that data to track your training, compare rides, and work with a coach, those differences can matter.

The big problem is that sticky watts don’t necessarily add the same amount to every ride. A steady climb with little coasting might show no difference. But a ride with lots of corners, stop signs, descents, or short, hard efforts followed by coasting could produce a much larger one. That makes it harder to compare rides or judge how much work you actually did.

The easiest way to check is to record the same ride on two cycling computers paired to the same power meter. You don’t necessarily need to buy a second computer. If a friend has one you can borrow, pair both to your power meter and record a ride with a few clear transitions from pedaling to coasting.

Alternatively, you can look closely at the power files your head unit generates. Do a couple of hard efforts, like sprints, where you stop pedaling at the end, then zoom in on those sections. Look for a flat section where one computer continues recording the same power value for several seconds after the other has dropped to zero.

And yes, I know that I’m definitely in some deep weeds over here, and it can be tough to argue that a cycling computer recording a few extra watts is a huge problem worth tackling. For many riders, it might not matter at all. But the current crop of cycling computers is also the most expensive we’ve ever seen. These devices are marketed and sold as precision training tools, and accurate data recording is central to that. These devices should do that, and riders shouldn’t have to question it.

#8774. Our 30 Unwritten Rules of Triathlon

Tim Heming outlines the comical 30 unwritten rules of triathlon that every athlete should know. (Photo: Challenge Family)

Like a lot of sports, triathlon is full of rules. For example, you’re not allowed to cut the course, have a motor on your bike, curse at officials, punch a rival, or, most craven of all, have fewer than three safety pins on your race number in France.

However, and particularly helpful for beginners, there are plenty more unwritten rules that we need to be aware of. Some of them, we’ve helpfully outlined below:

1. Procrastination is Expensive — Swear you’ll sign up at the early bird rate, procrastinate, and then find out your chosen Ironman sold out within 24 hours anyway.

2. Forever Alone — The training paradox. The more you do triathlons, the more all your friends are triathletes, and the more you will train alone.

3. You Are Not Kristian — The Norwegian Method is to train more hours in a day than you do not train. For more training methods, see YouTube.

4. The Devil’s in the Details — Dedicate 20 hours a week to training for three months in the lead up to your A race. Spend zero minutes working on transition.

5. Shelve Twitter Hate — Write a mantra on your water bottle and start an Instagram account for reels, stories, and collabs. Don’t be an angry person on Twitter. That’s not cool.

6. Match at All Costs — Never sacrifice style for performance. Color-coded kit and equipment are essential, unless you’re going for garish retro, which is an acceptable look for 2026 only.

7. Weather or Not? — Check the weather forecast and water temperature before checking the weather forecast and water temperature, and then solicit opinions on what the weather and water temperature are likely to be on race day.

8. Wetsuit Your Worries Away — Convince yourself you can’t swim without a wetsuit/won’t be able to get your wetsuit off if it’s a wetsuit swim.

9. Experience Equals Complacency — The athlete guide must be studied with a focus that inversely correlates to how many races the athlete has done.

10. Selfie First, Reality Later — Take a selfie with the giant M-Dot “Ironman Is In Town” sign. Post this to social media as soon as you land, feigning a smile because although you’ve arrived, your bike hasn’t yet followed.

11. Hell’s Bells — Set three alarms minimum and then wonder why the first of them is going off as you force-feed yourself rice because you couldn’t sleep anyway.

12. Nothing Matters as Much as Everything — Take time to stare at your race tattoo, realize the transfer has only half stuck, and have a mild panic by convincing yourself you’ll be disqualified before the start.

13. Apply Liberally — Use sunscreen, making sure you miss a key patch of skin. It will show more of your suffering.

14. Pay it Forward — In the name of karma, offer to: a) Zip up someone’s wetsuit; b) Lend them a bike pump (even if it’s not yours); c) Thank everyone you see profusely and wish them all a great day.

15. Ride the Intake Earthquake — Increase your volume of carbohydrates per hour exponentially with the same dedication you had when you raced 15 years ago and were insistent on using only your 5% body fat as a fuel source.

16. Be a Bathroom Banterer — Talk with bravado about your trained ability to both pee in the swim and on the bike while you stand for an hour in a revolving porta potty line.

17. What’s Good for the Goose is Good for the Gander — Oops! You punched someone in the eye in the swim completely by accident. Also, the breaststroker you got stuck behind at the first buoy deliberately kicked you in the face.

18. Meditate on Aquatic Paradoxes — During the swim, reflect on: a) Whoever learned to swim as a kid is basically a cheater. Or b) “Why do triathletes swim so freaking slowly?”

19. Style Reigns — Replace existing drink bottles on the bike with those from the on-course sponsor. Call bottles bidons if you’ve ever watched a clip of the Tour de France.

20. The Refs Need You (Really) — Become militant about drafting and shout obscenities at a pack who: a). Aren’t in the race anyway; b) Are out for a gentle social weekend ride; c) Are still moving faster than you.

21. Ride the Highs and Lows — When you are riding downhill, you think you will win. When you are riding uphill, you think you will come last.

22. Roll the Dice — Breathe a sigh of relief when you complete the bike leg without puncturing because you haven’t practiced changing tires for five years.

23. Don’t be Patronizing Pat — If you pass someone on the run, resist the urge to tap them encouragingly on the back. One athlete’s chirpy come-on is another athlete’s patronizing pat. And if you must do it, always avoid the backside.

24. Leave Self-Awareness Back at the Hotel — Do something in the finish chute that in any other walk of life you would find cringey. This includes sweaty mess marriage proposals to a long-suffering partner who has a cooked neck from staring at a race tracker for the past 14 hours.

25. Be Congratulating Carl — Always congratulate the first person you see at the finish. However hollow-eyed your expression or soiled your tri suit. It’s your duty to have that mutual moment with a complete stranger.

26. The Rules of Race Photography are Unbending — Acknowledge that official race photographs only ever capture: 1. Grotesque faces. 2: When you “briefly” sat up out of aero. 3. Ugly heel strikes

27. You’re the Best — Use multiple filters of the race results, including but not limited to age-groups, disciplines (including transitions), and nationalities to claim a top-10 position at some aspect of your race. If you rode a road bike, you can also disqualify everyone who rode a TT/tri bike.

28. Brutality Reigns — Include the word “brutal” at least three times during any social media race report.

29. There Are Steps — Once you have finished your first sprint triathlon, take the following actions (in order): a) Sign up for an Ironman, b) Sign up for a Hyrox, c) Advertise your coaching services.

30. Triathlon = Procrastination (Always) — Finally, swear you’ll sign up at the early bird rate, procrastinate, and then find out your chosen Ironman sold out within 24 hours anyway.

Visit the Iberia Plus website and locate their published off-peak date chart for your target route. Off-peak windows typically include January through March and October through November. Confirm your travel dates fall within the off-peak range before committing points.

Log into your Iberia Plus account and search for business class award flights on your target dates. Look for flights priced at 34,000 Avios one-way. If availability is not showing, try shifting dates by 1-2 days within the off-peak window.

Once you confirm availability, transfer points from Chase UR, Amex MR, Capital One, Citi ThankYou, or Marriott Bonvoy. Chase and Amex transfers are typically instant. Allow 1-2 business days for others.

Complete the booking through the Iberia website using your Avios balance. Unlike many partner awards, Iberia off-peak bookings can be made entirely online without calling. Select your seat during the booking process.

Madrid is a natural hub for onward travel. Consider booking a separate low-cost carrier flight or Avios short-haul to Barcelona, Lisbon, or Seville. Iberia's short-haul Avios pricing is also excellent for intra-Europe connections.

Picture this: you're settling into a fully flat bed on an Iberia Airbus A350-900, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Spanish wine in hand, Madrid a few hours away. The cabin is quiet, the seat is wide, and you're sleeping your way to Europe in genuine business class comfort. The person next to you in economy paid $900 for their ticket. You paid $900 in cash too — except your $900 covered taxes, fees, and a couple of nice dinners in Madrid. The flights themselves cost you 34,000 Iberia Avios. That's the magic of this redemption, and once you see it, you can't unsee it. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community light up: a round-trip business class ticket from JFK to Madrid on Iberia regularly retails for **$2,500 to $5,000** in cash. At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Europe in a lie-flat seat for fewer points than most domestic first class awards

Here's the insight that separates travelers who occasionally use points from those who systematically fly business class to Europe for nearly free: Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency, but they operate on completely different award charts.

Most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios. They know that BA prices awards by distance, and they know that BA is notorious for hefty fuel surcharges that can turn a "free" business class flight into a $700+ fees bill. So they write off transatlantic Avios redemptions as not worth it.

That's the mistake. Iberia — a fellow Oneworld carrier and Avios partner — publishes its own off-peak award chart for flights operated on Iberia metal (Iberia aircraft, Iberia flight numbers). Flights from the US to Madrid, when booked through Iberia Plus (not British Airways Executive Club), price out at 34,000 Avios one-way in business class during off-peak periods. That's the same Avios currency, same points you can transfer from Chase, but priced under Iberia's more favorable structure.

The fuel surcharge situation is also materially better on Iberia-operated flights booked through Iberia Plus than BA-operated flights booked through BA. Taxes and fees are generally moderate — you're looking at a few hundred dollars in fees rather than the $600–$700+ that sometimes plagues British Airways award bookings.

Off-peak windows are specific. Iberia defines off-peak as January through March and October through November. Mark those months. Outside of those windows, pricing steps up, and the sweet spot math starts to erode.

The transfer path is straightforward. Iberia Plus is a 1:1 transfer partner with Chase Ultimate Rewards, and transfers are instant — a critical advantage when you're chasing limited award availability. You search, you find the seat, you transfer, you book. No waiting 3–5 days for points to land and watching the seat disappear.

Marriott Bonvoy is also a transfer partner (3:1 ratio, 1–5 days), but the math there is less favorable and the speed is slower. Chase Ultimate Rewards is your primary earning vehicle for this redemption.

One important structural note: Avios are shareable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts — meaning if you've been accumulating BA Avios, you can move them to an Iberia Plus account to access Iberia's off-peak pricing. This opens the door even if you've been building your Avios balance through the British Airways credit card or BA partners. The accounts need to be linked through the Avios household account feature, but it's a powerful tool that many travelers overlook.

Finally, keep the expiry rule in mind: Iberia Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A single small transaction — even buying a few Avios — resets the clock. Don't let your points die quietly in an unused account.

If you don't already have one, go to iberia.com and sign up for a free Iberia Plus account. This takes about five minutes. Write down your membership number — you'll need it for the transfer step. Make sure your name matches your passport exactly to avoid issues at check-in.

Go to iberia.com and select "Book with Avios" in the award booking section. Enter your route (e.g., JFK to MAD) and select your travel dates. Critically, target off-peak months: January through March, and October through November. These are the windows where the 34,000 Avios one-way business class pricing applies.

Search one-way first. Iberia's search tool will show you available Avios seats color-coded by price — you're looking for the off-peak pricing tier. If you see 34,000 Avios for business class, that's your seat. Note the specific flight number and date before doing anything with your points.

Before transferring a single point, click through the booking to see the full taxes and fees. Iberia charges moderate fees on transatlantic awards — generally more reasonable than British Airways — but you want to know the number. Confirm you're comfortable with the cash portion before proceeding.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards portal at ultimaterewards.com. Navigate to "Transfer to Travel Partners" and select Iberia Plus. Transfer exactly 34,000 points (or the amount required for your specific itinerary). Transfers from Chase to Iberia Plus are 1:1 and instant — your Avios will appear in your Iberia Plus account within minutes.

Go back to iberia.com with your Iberia Plus account logged in. Confirm the award seat is still showing (it should be — you moved fast). Complete the booking using your Avios balance. Pay the taxes and fees with a card that earns well on travel or general spend.

Award space on popular routes can be tight. Here's how to improve your odds:

Most airline programs charge the same award price year-round or use dynamic pricing that moves with demand. Iberia is unusual because it publishes an explicit off-peak calendar with fixed lower pricing during specific date ranges. Off-peak pricing applies to the flight date, not the booking date, so you can book an off-peak flight months in advance and lock in the lower rate. The off-peak discount is roughly 50% compared to peak pricing on the same route. This creates a planning advantage for flexible travelers who can target specific travel windows. Combined with the fact that Avios transfer from five major credit card programs, it is one of the most accessible premium redemptions in the loyalty landscape.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers are concrete.

It's mid-October — peak fall travel season for most Europeans, but squarely within Iberia's off-peak award window (October through November). You've found award space on IB6251, JFK to MAD, departing John F. Kennedy at 10:30 PM and arriving at Madrid Barajas the following afternoon. The aircraft is an Airbus A350-900 — one of the best long-haul platforms in the sky.

The cash price for this flight in business class: $3,200 one-way, as priced on iberia.com for that week. Round trip in business runs approximately $4,800–$6,000 depending on timing.

The Avios price: 34,000 Iberia Avios plus approximately $250–$350 in taxes and fees.

Your CPP on this redemption: With a retail value of $3,200 and a cost of 34,000 points, you're extracting 9.4 cents per point — comfortably in the 7.4–14.7 cent range that defines this sweet spot as exceptional.

Now let's talk about what you're actually getting for those points. Iberia Business on the A350-900 features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration — meaning every passenger has direct aisle access. No climbing over a seatmate at 2 AM. The seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 73 inches. You'll have a personal entertainment screen, noise-canceling headphones, and amenity kit.

Before you board, you have access to Iberia's business class lounge at MAD (on the return) and partner lounges at JFK — typically the Iberia-operated space or a Oneworld partner lounge. The meal service on this transatlantic route reflects Spanish hospitality: proper courses, wine service, and a breakfast before landing.

For a couple traveling together, this redemption costs 68,000 Avios plus fees — a round figure that's very achievable through the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus alone. You land in Madrid rested, having slept in a flat bed over the Atlantic, having spent a fraction of what cash passengers paid. That's the FI travel rewards system working exactly as it should.

Do this: Book as close to 355 days out as possible for off-peak dates. Iberia releases award space up to 355 days in advance. The most reliable business class availability appears right when that window opens. If your target is January or February travel, set a calendar reminder for April or May of the prior year and search on Day 355. The seats won't last.

Do this: Transfer Avios from a BA account if you've been building there. If you've been earning BA Avios through the British Airways credit card or BA shopping portal, you don't need to start over. Avios are transferable across BA, Iberia, Aer Lingus, and Vueling accounts via the household account feature. Link the accounts, move the Avios to your Iberia Plus account, and access the off-peak pricing. This is an underused feature.

Do this: Earn points primarily through Chase Ultimate Rewards. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, and Ink Business Preferred all feed into the same Chase UR pool with a 1:1 instant transfer to Iberia Plus. For this redemption specifically, Chase is your most efficient earning engine. Use the welcome bonus from one of these cards as your foundation — a 60,000–100,000 point bonus gets you most of the way to two one-way business class seats.

Avoid this: Transferring points before confirming award space. Avios are transferred into Iberia Plus and can't be easily moved back or transferred to another program without complexity. Always confirm the exact flight, date, and availability BEFORE you initiate a transfer from Chase. The instant transfer speed from Chase means you can lock in availability quickly — but only once you've verified the seat exists.

Avoid this: Booking during peak periods expecting off-peak pricing. December, July, and August are not off-peak. The 34,000 Avios rate is specifically tied to Iberia's off-peak calendar (January–March and October–November). Outside those windows, pricing increases significantly and the CPP math deteriorates. Don't assume off-peak pricing applies year-round.

Do this: Keep your Iberia Plus account active. Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you're holding points for a future redemption, keep the account alive with a small transaction — even earning a few Avios through a partner purchase resets the clock for another 36 months.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want to experience genuine transatlantic business class — flat beds, real meal service, lounge access — without the $3,000–$5,000 cash outlay that normally makes that choice feel irresponsible on a FI journey.

You're a great fit for this redemption if:

This is also an excellent gateway redemption for families with older children who understand that off-peak travel timing is part of the strategy — though booking four or more business class seats requires significant Avios accumulation and tighter award availability.

For the FI community member who's disciplined about earning and has a Chase UR foundation, this is one of the cleanest business class sweet spots available anywhere in the transatlantic market.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty** — not because anything about it is technically complex, but because it requires you to navigate a few specific steps that most people haven't done before. **The main challenges are:** 1. **Awareness of the separate Iberia award chart.** Most travelers default to British Airways Avios and never discover that Iberia prices its own flights differently. Once you know this, it's not a challenge — it's an advantage. 2. **Award availability.** Iberia business class award seats on JFK–MAD are genuinely limited, especially as you get closer to the off-peak windows. You're competing with other knowledgeable award travelers. Availability is rated a 3 out of 5 for a reason — the seats are there, but you have to work for them. 3. **Account setup.** You need an Iberia Plus account separate from any BA account, and you need to navigate iberia.com's award search interface, which is functional but not as polished as some other programs. **Three tips to overcome these challenges:** - Search award space **355 days in advance** for maximum selection - Use **iberia.com directly** to search — it shows Iberia-operated availability most accurately - Keep the **Chase UR instant transfer** in your back pocket so you can act the moment you find space If you've ever transferred points to an airline and booked an award flight before, this will feel familiar. If this is your first time, expect to spend an evening learning the process — but the payoff is a flat-bed seat over the Atlantic for a fraction of its cash price. That's worth an evening.

Iberia Avios and British Airways Avios are the same currency and can be transferred between accounts for free. However, Iberia's award chart prices flights on Iberia metal differently than British Airways does. For flights to Madrid on Iberia-operated routes, booking through Iberia Plus is typically cheaper than through BA Executive Club.

No. Iberia's off-peak pricing applies only to Iberia-operated flights. British Airways has its own separate pricing structure through BA Executive Club. For flights to London, you would need to use BA Avios and their own award chart, which does not offer the same off-peak discount.

Yes. Iberia updates its off-peak calendar periodically, and the specific date ranges can shift by a few weeks. Always check the current published calendar before planning your trip. The general pattern of January-March and October-November as off-peak has been consistent, but exact boundaries vary.

Iberia long-haul business class features fully flat seats in a 1-2-1 configuration with direct aisle access on their A350 and A330 aircraft. The seats convert to a flat bed for sleeping. The food and wine service reflects Spanish culinary traditions, including Iberian ham and regional wines. It is a solid European business class product, comparable to Air France or Lufthansa.

Iberia Avios off-peak business class to Madrid is the most efficient way to fly business class to Europe on points. At 34,000 Avios one-way, it costs less than many domestic first class awards. The off-peak calendar rewards flexible travelers with a 50% discount, and the breadth of transfer partners means almost anyone with transferable points can access this redemption. If you can align your European travel with the off-peak windows, this sweet spot delivers exceptional value with minimal complexity.

#8766. Running Faster vs Running Longer: Which Should I Focus On First?

Both are key components of a smart training plan—but how you prioritize each one depends on your goal.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Runners have two main paths to choose from when it comes to running goals: run faster or run longer. Both will make you a stronger, fitter athlete—but training for one looks a little different than the other.

Should you focus on running faster to build power and strength, or should you go the distance to test your physical and mental stamina? There’s no right or wrong answer, but understanding the differences between these two approaches can help you make the most of your training.

Like so many questions in running, the answer depends on your current fitness level and your goals. But for most new runners, it’s generally better to start training to run longer.

“I think sometimes runners are quick to jump into trying to run all-out, whatever their goal race is, instead of just working toward being able to feel okay completing the distance first,” says Ruth Atkinson, VDOT-certified McKirdy Trained running coach based in Dallas. That means you probably want to think about the distance you want to cover first, whether you’re vying for your first 5K or have some shorter distances under your belt and are considering a half marathon or marathon.

There’s a saying in running: Start where you are. In other words, don’t put a time goal on a race when you start training. Instead, start training, see how your fitness improves as you get closer to race day, then set a time goal. Some research even indicates that building up your easy mileage will lead to better long-distance run performance compared to focusing on speed workouts: A study published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research in 2021, involving 84 male runners, found a correlation between volume of easy runs—not tempo runs, not interval training—with world-class long-distance running performance scores.

One of the most important benefits of gradually increasing your volume is training your tendons, ligaments, joints, and bones to withstand the repetitive impact of running without overtaxing them, which might lead to overuse injuries. “Starting with distance gives your body a chance to catch up to the muscular capacity you need to develop to stay healthy and move forward,” says New York-based Nike running coach Rebeka Stowe. It’s generally easier and faster for beginners to build aerobic capacity compared to muscle strength, so you have to give your muscles enough time to build that strength.

Once you have a solid aerobic base—the foundational fitness you need to sustain your training—you could shift to more of a speed focus.

Not all running has the same effects on your body. When you’re training for distance, most miles will be at a low-intensity effort. (When it comes to rate of perceived exertion, this would be about a 4 out of 10 effort, or lower, with 10 being all out.) That easy, conversational pace may not feel challenging—although it will help you develop mental toughness by teaching you how to push through fatigue and discomfort as the miles add up—but it’s stimulating important physiological adaptations that will improve your performance at faster paces.

For starters, you’re improving your cardiovascular capabilities. “Your heart is a muscle,” says Stowe. “By running at a slower pace, you’re building that muscle’s capacity to pump blood to the rest of your body so it can handle higher intensity work later.” As your heart’s stroke volume increases with training, it beats less frequently to supply the same amount of blood to the body—meaning it’s becoming more efficient.

Slower runs also train your slow twitch (type I) muscle fibers, which allow you to sustain your pace over longer distances. These muscle fibers have a higher density of mitochondria and greater capillary density, both of which help you maintain your energy level.

In fact, aerobic exercise increases the number of mitochondria in your cells, according to research published in the American Journal of Physiology—Endocrinology and Metabolism, and can increase capillary density by more than 25 percent, an older study in Journal of Atherosclerosis and Thrombosis found. The more mitochondria you have, the more energy you can produce, and the greater your capillary density, the better blood flow to your working muscles. Both of those benefits translate to improved performance at faster speeds.

Speed work, on the other hand, acts almost like strength training, developing your muscles as you work against increased ground reaction forces.

“Challenging your body to run at a faster pace is going to call on more muscle fibers,” says Stowe. In this case, you’re working fast twitch (type II) muscle fibers, which are best suited for short, explosive efforts. These fast-twitch fibers also come into play at the end of a race for your finishing kick.

Picking up the pace also improves your cardiovascular capacity, but in a different way than easy running. Working at a higher intensity increases your VO2 max, “the maximum amount of oxygen that your body can use during exercise,” explains Atkinson. “The more you practice running at this pace, the easier it will be to translate that into holding faster paces for longer periods of time.”

Training for speed will also improve your lactate threshold—the intensity level at which lactate accumulates in the blood faster than you can remove it, leading to fatigue—so you can improve your endurance at faster paces.

To gain these benefits, you can base the pace needed off of your 5K time. If you don’t know your race pace for that distance, you can just go out and run 3.1 miles as hard as you can—it should be an 8 or 9 effort level on a scale of 1 to 10. VO2 max pace is a bit faster than 5K pace, while lactate threshold pace is a bit slower than 5K pace. (Keep in mind speed workouts aren’t always built around just these specific paces. A good training plan will have you holding speeds from mile pace or faster all the way up to marathon pace and slower, depending on your goals.)

Speed training also positively affects the density and structure of your bones, and may potentially prevent age-related bone loss, according to a research review published in 2023 in Sechenov Medical Journal—further bulletproofing your body against overuse injuries.

Another benefit of speed training: It requires a lot less time than building volume, which helps runners who are balancing training with other obligations.

When you train for distance, your workouts will focus on gradually building up the time or mileage you run. Long runs at a conversational pace will be the cornerstone of your plan, along with some moderate-intensity runs and recovery days.

“If you’re running four days a week, you’d have one day of speed and three easy days with higher volume, including a long run,” says Atkinson. Your speed workout would typically include longer intervals at goal pace, adds Stowe. “You should do a good majority of your speed volume at half marathon or marathon pace so that you become more efficient—and more comfortable—holding that pace,” she explains.

The goal, when you’re training to run longer, is to improve your aerobic endurance and teach your body to handle the physical demands of extended activity. As you progress, you’ll increase your weekly mileage to build the stamina you need to go the distance.

Training for speed generally aims to improve your pace over shorter distances. You might run shorter, more intense workouts but with more recovery time between efforts. Let’s say you’re training for a fast 5K race: “You would ease into it by doing 200-meter and 400-meter reps at goal 5K pace, because you’re not going to be able to sustain that pace over longer distances yet,” says Stowe. “As your training continues, you progress to 800s, mile repeats, even 2K repeats—you can work your way up to holding that goal pace in smaller chunks.”

If you’re still running four days a week, your training plan might include three easy runs and a speed workout, or two days with speed and two that are easy, Atkinson says. Your focus will be on maximizing your cardiovascular capacity, running form, and the ability to push your body to sustain those faster efforts. “The quality of your workouts will be a little bit harder, which means the quantity will be a little bit less to keep everything balanced,” she explains.

A good training plan incorporates speed and volume, because your body has different energy systems that respond to different stimuli.

“Think of it like a recipe,” says Stowe. “If you’re supposed to mix salt and sugar into something but you forget to do one, you’re not going to get the desired outcome. The taste is going to be off, right? If you want to optimize your outcome, you have to have speed and volume as part of your training, so you’re developing all of your systems.”

Starting with distance will help you build the foundation you need to develop speed. “If you spend a dedicated amount of time increasing your volume, you’re going to build a pretty robust aerobic system,” says Atkinson. “When you add speed work to that, you’re learning how to turn your legs over faster and become more efficient at faster paces. Then, you have the aerobic system in place to be able to hold the faster paces you can now run.”

For most runners, it’s a cycle. You may spend four to six months training for distance, and then two to four months working on speed; then you layer endurance back in and combine the two.

Both speed and distance training have their own set of benefits, and you can always mix and match, choosing what fits your current goals and lifestyle. Whether you’re training to run faster or longer, each step will bring you closer to becoming the strongest version of yourself.
