#8759. The 8 Best Altra Running Shoes for Runners Who Hate Cramped Toes and Want to Try Zero-Drop

Altra is known for its women-specific fit, wide toebox, and zero-drop cushioning. We recommend the best Altra shoes—including those with a 4mm offset—out now.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Editor’s Note, November 10, 2026: Need some support trying low drop? The Altra Experience Form is now 24% off—but inventory is low, so stock up now!

Altra holds a special place in my heart because one of the first shoes I reviewed after I was hired at Runner’s World was the brand’s now-discontinued Instinct/Intuition 4.5. Altra was founded in 2009 by high school running buddies Golden Harper and Brian Beckstead. Turns out the Instinct/Intuition was pivotal to Altra establishing itself in the running industry. It was the first model Altra launched in 2011.

Since my introduction to Altra, I’ve witnessed its evolution; the brand formerly known for strictly selling zero-drop shoes (when forefoot and heel cushioning are equal) has added models with a 4mm drop. This move has drawn the zero-drop-curious to the Altra way.

Looking for a zero-drop daily trainer → Altra Torin 9 (Men’s/Women’s)

In need of stability → Altra Experience Form (Men’s/Women’s)

Curious to try low-drop → Altra Experience Flow 3 (Men’s/Women’s)

Shopping for a low-drop trail shoe → Altra Experience Wild 3 (Men’s/Women’s)

Racing a marathon → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s)

Logging long runs → Altra Fwd Via 2 (Men’s/Women’s)

Wanting a true racing flat → Altra Escalante 5 (Men’s/Women’s)

A lover of gnarly trails → Altra Lone Peak 9+ (Men’s/Women’s)

Balanced Cushioning, which refers to the shoe’s heel-to-toe drop, or lack thereof. Altra designs most of its shoes with no drop, meaning your foot sits flat rather than sloping downward from heel to toe. According to Altra, this can help promote your natural stride and encourage a lower-impact landing—because the heel isn’t as beefed up, you’re less likely to land on it.

Altra also introduced its 4mm line of shoes so runners can ease into zero-drop with an offset that’s approximately two stacked nickels.

The first time I ran in Altras, I couldn’t help feeling like I was wearing clown shoes. Unbox a pair of Altras and you’ll see that the forefoot is much wider than on other shoes; the enlarged, anatomical toe box allows the foot to expand and gives the toes room to splay. Altra now has three different foot shapes: original (the widest), standard, and slim (the narrowest).

Wide-foot runners and runners with bunions appreciate the roominess in the toe area. But all runners can benefit from wearing Altra’s foot-shaped trainers. A narrow toebox that cramps your toes can negatively affect your performance (and set you up for injuries).

The company uses three main cushioning materials in its shoes: Ego, Ego Max, and Ego Pro.

Ego: Compared to traditional EVA, this foam provides a springier feel and more durability.

Ego Max: A foam made of compression-molded EVA and tuned for a softer feel than Ego, but it isn’t as responsive.

Ego Pro: Altra’s top-shelf foam made of thermoplastic elastomers (TPE) formed in a supercritical fluid process. It’s the brand’s lightest and most responsive cushioning material.

P35X: Altra’s new and improved version of Ego foam that’s lighter and more efficient.

Altra’s stability tech is its guide rail, which is a layer of dense midsole foam that is raised on the medial side. The guide rail serves as a “bumper” that helps counter overpronation during your stride.

Altra’s women’s shoes are built on a women’s-specific last to match the biomechanics of female feet. These shoes are narrower through the heel and midfoot and better accommodate women’s generally longer arches.

Since my introduction to Altra as a new hire at Runner’s World in 2018, I have tested several models by the brand, appreciating the shoes’ generous toe room on my wide feet. I have tested all of the shoes in this buying guide and delved into the feedback of our 350-plus shoe testers. These local runners present an inclusive testing pool, ranging in gait patterns, arch heights, and experience levels.

*All weights are for men’s 10 and women’s 8.

The Torin has undergone a revamp with its ninth iteration—but rest assured, all these changes are welcomed upgrades.

The shoe has a new Vibram outsole, which inspired our testers to take the shoe off the road and onto the trail. “I felt that the shoe performed best on a packed dirt/trail surface where it felt like it had a great traction and springy push off. Those trail runs were at a 7:00 to 7:30 pace,” said tester Steven Blasi.

On the road and off, the Torin 9 is bouncier and softer too. Altra’s P35X midsole makes for a more cushioned ride without silencing ground feel. The support makes the shoe a great entry into zero-drop for newbies.

Lastly, the fit is more accommodating. The non-gusseted tongue provides a roomier fit for those with high insteps.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

The Experience Form provides stability when you need it with Altra’s guide rail. Acting as a “bumper” on the medial side, the feature lends support to overpronators and neutral runners, alike.

“I liked the overall stability and comfort of the shoe,” said Anthony Dentino, a heel-striker who runs with a neutral gait. “The shoe was firm but provided excellent cushioning throughout, especially in the heel. Because of its weight, this is not a shoe that I would suggest for speedwork or racing but it is an excellent training shoe.”

Another favorite feature was the shoe’s hardiness and trustworthiness in inclement weather.

“I wore them multiple times in the rain and on some snowy surfaces, but felt like they provided good traction every time,” said overpronator Alyssa Dever. “Not only that, they did not soak through easily in the rain, and kept my feet warm in cold temperatures (some sub-20-degree runs).”

Shop Men’s at rei.com Shop Women’s at rei.com

If switching to zero-drop still sounds like taking a major leap, you can opt for running in the Experience Flow 3 before you go for a spin in the Torin 8. The Experience Flow has a 4mm offset, which is approximately the same depth of two nickels stacked on top of each other. The heel lift is subtle, allowing you to ease into running in a low-drop shoe.

Testers loved the versatility of the shoe, appreciating its supportive Altra Ego midsole. For some, it hit that Goldilocks sweet spot of feeling not too firm, nor too soft.

“I loved that it was a not a minimalist shoe, but wasn’t the huge cloud cushion kind either,” said tester Chris Greg. “It was a happy medium between the two where I felt connected to the ground but was offered plenty of support to make my 5-mile runs smooth.”

Others described the cushioning as having just the right amount of “squishiness.”

“I really loved how much cushioning these shoes had,” said tester Mary Hartnett. “It made my runs feel so much easier and ‘squishier’ compared to other shoes I’ve used. This extra softness was a huge help during my training because I actually felt excited to put them on every morning, and my feet didn’t feel as tired afterward.”

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

We’ve loved the Experience Wild since its first iteration. The shoe is outfitted for technical trails, offering protection with a toe sweep, gaiter attachment points, and a grippy MaxTrac outsole that can handle loose, uneven terrain. It’s also a great option for those who run on bridle paths and groomed rail trails. The Experience Wild 3 is flexible, has an accommodating wide fit in the midfoot and toe area, and a padded tongue that makes the fit snug and enclosed, so pebbles and sand can be kept out.

The biggest update to the Experience Wild 3 is the mesh upper, which provides a more secure fit and more breathability.

“V3 takes the shoe to the next level with a redesigned upper that fits more generously but doesn’t make you feel like you are swimming around, a more plush cushioning that absorbs firmer ground yet remaining stable, and a lug pattern on the MaxTrac outsole that I felt was superior to each of the previous models in terms of grip,” said tester John Mikovits.

The Experience Wild 3+ ($165) is also available and has a Vibram Megagrip outsole.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

The Vanish Carbon 3 feels like a true super while preserving Altra’s fit and feel. The racing shoe is the first in its line with a 4mm offset; the Altra shoe team realized their super shoe needed a drop so they wouldn’t be outmatched by competitors. Altra’s running economy tests showed the Vanish Carbon 3 had 2.6 percent better running economy compared to the Vanish Carbon 2.

A carbon plate is sandwiched between FastRce, which is pure PEBA. The plate has a split big toe to allow for engagement and power. All this is housed in an upper with Altra’s signature roomy toebox that provides generous wiggle room for your toes to splay.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

As of updating this buying guide, I only just laced up in the Fwd Via 2 after meeting with Altra at the Runner’s World Shoe Summit before the NYC Marathon. The original Fwd Via was an instant favorite from first run. The shoe has a rocker profile and high cushioning, making the low heel-to-toe drop easier to get used to if you’re a zero-drop virgin. It’s great for long runs and recovery runs, and has a generous bed of foam for run/walkers.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

It’s been two and a half years since the release of the Escalante 4—but the Escalante 5 makes that length of time worth the wait.

Nothing has dramatically changed with the Escalante 5: same roomy toebox, same breathable knit upper, same Ego midsole, and same 24 mm stack height. Instead of fully revamping the shoe, the Altra team refined it with a few tweaks.

The strobel and sockliner are made of TPEE for even more comfort. In this way, you still get plenty of ground feel in this minimalistic, lightweight trainer, but with added comfort and support. The outsole also has more rubber to enhance traction and durability.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

The Lone Peak 9+ is the first iteration of the shoe with a Vibram Megagrip outsole. This makes the shoe have outstanding traction on wet or dry surfaces. RW Tester feedback confirms Vibram Megagrip’s traction on uneven, slippery terrain.

Said tester Shelby Brett, “I greatly appreciate that the lugs on the shoe are significant and that they go in multiple directions, again adding to my confidence underfoot.”

The shoe has a durable ripstop upper and an extra eyelet for a more locked-in fit. Testers loved the ground feel of the Lone Peak 9+, saying the shoe had the perfect balance of cushioning and protection. Another highlight was that spacious toebox.

Shop Men’s at altrarunning.com | Shop Women’s at altrarunning.com

We recommend starting slow and short if it’s your first time running in zero-drop shoes. Shoes with a drop have more cushioning in the heel. If you’re a heel-striker, you may need to run in a zero-drop shoe with a higher stack height to provide more support under the heel area. Try Altra’s 4mm shoes first to become accustomed to a lower-drop shoe.

What is the difference between Altra’s guide rail and Brooks’s guide rails?

Altra’s guide rail runs along the medial side of the shoe, acting as a bumper and preventing your foot from collapsing during sharp turns or if your feet roll inward during your gait cycle (overpronation).

Brooks’s guide rails are on the medial and lateral sides of the shoe. Like Altra’s guide rail, the guide rails also provide stability when you need it, making the shoes supportive for overpronators and neutral runners. The guide rails act as bumpers, helping align the knee and ankle.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. #8758. The Bivo Trio Mini Keeps Finding a Place on Our Bikes When the Temperatures Begin to Dip—Here’s Why

In a crowded category, the Bivo Trio Bottle ends up in our bottle cages for colder rides.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Your water bottles have probably frozen at least once if you ride outside in cold weather. Usually, it’s only a thin layer of ice on top or a clogged nozzle, but that’s enough to be annoying. If you ride at low enough temperatures with standard plastic bottles filled with plain water, it will inevitably happen. However, it’s important to stay hydrated on winter rides.

There are proven ways to keep your bottles from freezing—or carry hot beverages on rides. Hot chocolate, coffee, tea, or Skratch Labs’ apple cider will warm your soul and lift your mood. And nothing hits better than a coffee stop in the middle of a cold winter ride, especially when conditions are dreary or sloppy.

Stainless insulated bottles broke into cycling about five years ago and have since exploded in popularity. They’re a proven way to keep water and hydration mix cool on the hottest summer days, and they can also keep hot drinks warm for many miles on winter rides.

The Bivo Trio Bottle, available in raw stainless steel and silicone-covered stainless steel versions, has become a bottle of choice on cold-weather rides. Read on to find out why, plus tips to prevent your bottles from freezing this winter.

Cyclists have many different methods (often handed down from one generation of riders to the next) to help prevent frozen bottles. One simple solution is to start your ride with hot water. However, depending on the temperature and ride length, this can also freeze.

Using insulated plastic bottles, adding a high-sodium drink mix, and wearing a hydration pack or vest under a riding jacket are all tricks I’ve used (with varying degrees of success) to keep my bottles from freezing. And some riders still swear by adding a shot of booze to their bidon. However, while these methods may prevent icing, they still result in a cold beverage during your ride.

It’s hard to miss the growing popularity of stainless steel water bottles in cycling. Their use has boomed in the last few seasons as more riders have become concerned about microplastic contamination. Plus, these metal bidons, particularly the Bivo bottles, are in the cages of many cycling influencers.

Stainless bottles typically feature a vacuum-sealed double-wall design with a coated outer and a bare stainless inner layer. Since metal bottles are rigid, you cannot squeeze them like plastic bottles. (It takes some getting used to if you haven’t ridden them before.) And while stainless bottles are much heavier than plastic models, they are heavy-duty and almost indestructible—they dent and scratch but rarely break.

Bivo is the trend-setting stainless option and commonly available from retailers like REI, Backcountry, Amazon, or your local bike shop. The Insulated Mini we tested is 17 ounces and costs $44, or opt for the 21-ounce model for $5 more.

I have ridden with insulated bottles at several points in my cycling life. But until last summer, I usually stuck with non-insulated plastic bottles for most of my rides, regardless of air temperature.

Generally, I prefer the feel of a regular bottle; 22-ounce Specialized Purist bottles are my go-to, and I occasionally carry a 10-ounce Purist Maker mug for a mid-ride coffee break. But I often skip stainless insulated bottles because they aren’t squeezable and weigh noticeably more than plastic bidons.

However, before a recent ride on a cold and blustery day, I filled an insulated bottle with hot chocolate and was pleased to have a warm treat throughout my 90-minute ride. So, like my insulated bottle test last summer, I applied a little science to see which insulated stainless bottles performed best in cold temps.

For this test, I gathered several popular metal insulated bottles. First, I evaluated the bottles by measuring water temperature over three hours in subfreezing conditions. Then, I used them on rides in cold weather to determine which worked best from a functional perspective.

While the intent was somewhat scientific, I also strove to be practical—these are tests anyone can do at home. This testing was not performed in a controlled environment or with professional-level, calibrated equipment.

Since it was below 32 degrees outside, I was able to perform outdoor freeze testing. Like my summer insulated bottle tests, I filled the selected bottles with 400 grams of tap water (heated to 212 degrees for this test instead of chilled water used in summer). Then I placed the filled bottles on my front porch in subfreezing temperatures; I did this after sunset so sunlight would not warm the bottles. Every 30 minutes, I checked and recorded the water temperature of each bottle, in the same order each time, with a digital food thermometer.

Following the initial three-hour test period, the bottles remained overnight in sub-freezing temperatures for an additional nine hours. This tested whether the contents would stay warm for a full 12 hours (as per some bottle makers’ claims). Additionally, for reference, I subjected a Purist Maker tumbler (with 200 grams of water), an insulated plastic bottle, and a standard plastic bottle to the same tests.

The following day, I evaluated the bottles’ on-bike performance on a short loop in my neighborhood. I tested their use with standard and lobster-claw gloves (such as holding, opening caps, removing them from cages) and their nozzles’ function while drinking hot coffee (a medium-roast pour-over with some oat milk for my tests 😉).

The results were clear: Insulated stainless bottles work very well in cold weather. They keep your beverage hot for an hour-long ride in 30-degree temps. For longer rides, your drink will experience some heat loss but will remain drinkably warm for three hours. The insulated metal bottles performed notably better than plastic bottles (insulated and non-insulated) for the full duration of the test.

After about three hours of exposure in the cold, the Bivo Insulated Trio Mini kept my coffee at a warm 119.8 degrees. This is only slightly below coffee expert James Hoffmann’s recommended coffee-drinking temp of 122 to 129 degrees. (Although I’m not sure Hoffmann would be pleased drinking three-hour-old brew.) In 12-hour testing, none of the metal bottles froze. Most bottles finished at room temperature after 12 hours outside in freezing temperatures.

On the bike, the Bivo valve works great, and the bottle texture isn’t overly slippery. The bottle shape is compatible with most cages, though it fits best in the Arundle Sport cage recommended by Bivo.

Nozzle Shield: Look for bottles with a cap that protects the nozzle. Typically, I’m not a fan of these shields when riding in warm weather—they flop around and get in the way when drinking. However, in the winter, caps keep road salt and slush off the bottle’s nozzle, and they also help prevent icing. Ones with a removable plastic or rubber shield are easier to clean; plus, you can use the bottles without the cap on warm days.

Vapor Pressure: Many of the tested bottles carry a warning about using liquids hotter than 180 degrees. This is to avoid scalding and burns from pressurized hot water when the cap or nozzle is opened. With insulated bottles, hot liquid heats the air inside the bottle enough to spray potentially near-boiling water into your mouth or onto your body.

Avoid this by letting your hot beverage cool slightly before pouring it into your bottle. For long rides (when using two bottles of hot drinks), save the hotter bottle for later in the day. This way, it has time to cool to a drinkable temperature.

Cage Compatibility: Since they do not deform or flex, metal bottles don’t pair with every bottle cage. Some stainless bottles have a loose fit in cages (bottles can even eject on rough roads), and some cage shapes do not allow some metal bottles to sit correctly, causing annoying rattling and buzzing while riding. Other cage-bottle pairings are so tight that it’s hard to remove the bottle while riding.

My advice: Check that your cages work before dropping up to $100 for new bottles that won’t fit. Some brands have specific cage recommendations on their sites. You can also read user reviews for the compatibility of different bottles and cages. Also, be sure to check the overall bottle height to be sure it fits in your frame.

Dropped Bottles: I do not recommend using metal bottles in mass-start situations; use plastic bidons for big group rides or races. When a metal bottle is ejected from a cage on a bump, or you drop one (as is prone to happen with cold hands or when wearing bulky gloves), it ricochets off the road surface more than a plastic bottle. And while metal makes these bottles more durable, they do not burst open on impact or crush if hit by other riders.

Bivo shook up the bottle market when it launched its stainless steel bottles. The small Richmond, Vermont-based company launched insulated bottles shortly after, and cyclists have fallen in love with them. They work well, look good, and don’t have a funky taste.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8757. Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.)

The benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”

Well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next big upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.)

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

Another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

Damn that is exciting! Pedestrianism FTW!

Yay! I’m thrilled to read about a city of the future, and I look forward to hearing more when you spend the winter there. I gave them my email address so I could hear more in the future.

Mr. Money Mustache April 8, 2023, 6:43 pm

Believe it or not, this is not a big problem in Phoenix and most other big desert cities. They have plenty of water for domestic use. It’s agriculture that uses the lion’s share of fresh water – about 80% of it in the Western US. Then our other industrial uses, then our houses are down near the bottom.

One major improvement in places like Phoenix and Las Vegas versus the rest of the country is that they have managed to mostly eliminate suburban lawns. A single patch of lawn watered in the desert will use more than an entire household, so as soon as you remove that you have made the whole city more sustainable.

Alas, here in the Denver area the lawn with the big sprinkler system still seems to be in style, despite the fact that our summer climate very closely resembles a real desert. The grass will die within a week or two if you leave it unwatered, which I think would be a great idea in most cases. There’s lots of cool stuff you can do with river rocks and native flowers and Yucca plants that takes almost no water to sustain!

Very accurate, MMM! I’ve got a good friend who works for whatever they call the “water” department of the city of Mesa (right next to Tempe), and whenever I bring up the metro Phoenix water supply issue, he basically says “we’ll be fine, but things will have to change with respect to agriculture in the southwest and lawns/golf courses”.

I worried about it for years, but a bit of research and several articles in the NYT helped calm me down. Here’s one: https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/05/22/climate/colorado-river-water.html .

TLDR: We’re going to have to continue to evolve what we raise/grow/eat to balance the demands on our planet, especially considering climate change (to the surprise of practically nobody reading MMM)

I was in Rome and I LOVE their car culture. If you drive a moped scooter in Italy, you get special traffic-bypassing privilege; such as driving on the centerline to bypass gridlock. It is perfectly safe because everyone is aware of it. Most city streets are primarily WALKED, with cars being a secondary form of transport. If you want to travel far, the train is less than $20, it goes 170mph, and is very enjoyable to travel on. Also, the cars are almost all manual transmission…. This has nothing to do with efficiency, but it is a very cool part of the culture. After spending a week there, walking over 10 miles per day, and riding around the countryside on a vespa, coming back to the USA felt sad. Everything is so spread out, and if I want to go 100+ miles, I’m forced to drive. Trains are incredible. Imagine taking a 170mph train and a folding bike to San Diego for the weekend. I’d be there a LOT.

I live in Madrid (Spain) now it’s the city center is much like you describe it. It was built centuries ago (started 500 years ago and evolved in tiers). Obviously, it was not designed for cars. There are still cars moving around, but it’s clear that they are the 2nd grade citizens here. Most transport is on foot and a super efficient metro system. Then, the medium and long range rail lines. Most people living here don’t have nor need a car.

I also live in Spain (A Coruña) and I was thinking the same as you Amir.

This video is good summary of Spanish cities from the perspective of someone from a North American”

‘Pedestrianized Streets Are Good, So What Are We Even Doing?’ https://youtu.be/7BRvk-_wM6U

In my city in Canada, people were protesting against the concept of 15 minute cities proposed by the municipal government. The protesters believe it is part of the plan but an authoritarian global world order power(s) that aim to confine people to geographic prisons and ban cars.

15 minute cities are a very sensible idea which became subject to a lot of mass hysteria a few years ago. Hopefully some common sense on the matter has returned.

#8756. The Best Whey Protein Powders of 2025, According to a Certified Sports Nutrition Coach

Whey protein powders are a convenient way to up your daily protein intake. We tested over 50 to choose the best whey protein on the market.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Whey protein powder is a popular supplement because it’s a simple and effective way to increase daily protein intake.

Whey is a complete protein that contains all nine essential amino acids our bodies need to build muscle. Whey protein also supplies the body with branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), like leucine, which help promote muscle growth (1).

We consulted Pete Nastasi, a certified nutrition coach (C.N.C.), to help us find the best whey protein powders on the market.

Here, we break down the different types of whey protein powders available (concentrate, isolate, and hydrolysate), which types will work best for you, and what nutrition information to look for. Plus, we’ve tested over 50 protein powders to help us create the list of our top picks.

Medical disclaimer: This article is intended for educational and informational purposes only. It is not intended as a substitute for medical advice. For health advice, contact a licensed healthcare provider.

We chose products for our list of the best whey protein powders based on a number of factors reflected in our whey protein powder scoring methodology. These include:

We also receive input from our panel of expert contributors, which includes registered dietitians and highly credentialed experts in sports nutrition and exercise science.

No sugar, all protein—that’s what Transparent Labs set out to accomplish with its grass-fed whey protein isolate. This whey protein undergoes filtration (2), taking out the excess sugar, fat, carbs, and lactose so you’re giving your body the pure protein it needs to rebuild. Whey isolate has the highest protein concentration of the different types of protein powders, and this protein is a good option if you’re trying to reduce your carb and fat intake.

Transparent Labs’ Whey Protein Isolate packs 28 grams of protein into each serving—one of the highest on our list. We also like the flavor variety, including unique flavors like Cinnamon French Toast. Bonus: This protein isn’t too sweet, so you can mix it with fruit juice or add it to a fruit smoothie without feeling like you’re drinking a shake made with Fun Dip.

Sports Research Whey Protein is formulated with 6.9 grams of BCAAs, including 1,000 milligrams of L-leucine. Studies show leucine may help reduce delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS). Depending on flavor, this Informed Sport Certified protein powder is sweetened with stevia or sucralose, so those sensitive to these ingredients may need to steer clear.

Rachel Pasche says she has a protein shake for dessert some nights using the Dutch Chocolate flavor. “It might be too sweet for some people, but I honestly love the taste so much,” she says. “It’s my favorite flavor of protein powder I’ve ever tried.” She says the powder mixes well with water alone, with both a handheld mixer and in a shaker cup, noting there is some foam at the top that doesn’t last long and no clumping.

Additionally, Pasche says she sometimes feels bloated after whey protein shakes, but after six months of using Sports Research Whey, she has not experienced any bloat.

Why is grass-fed whey protein better? Studies show that dairy sourced from grass-fed cows has a higher concentration of whey proteins and amino acids (3), which may further support muscular training adaptations.

This Nutricost protein powder is non-GMO, gluten-free, and third-party tested. Whey protein concentrate, like this one, is often made with sunflower lecithin, an ingredient to help promote mixability. Testers also enjoy the taste and say this protein powder mixes well. “The taste was nostalgic; I’d liken it to Nesquik,” says tester Grant Smith. “And the mixability was on par with some of the better proteins I’ve had previously.” Smith was pleasantly surprised by the mixability of Nutricost Whey Protein, noting he didn’t find any small chunks of undissolved protein floating in his shake when mixed with milk.

After drinking most of his shake, Smith let a bit of the mixture sit for almost 10 minutes after initially mixing to test for separation. He noticed some slight separation between the protein and skim milk he mixed it with, but says it wasn’t enough to make the drink any less appealing.

The protein in Legion Athletics is certified to contain no banned substances by Labdoor, the gold standard of third-party lab testing. This helps ensure the protein isolate is in its purest, most nutritionally dense form without any interference from pesticides and growth hormones.

Additionally, Legion Athletics whey is filtered to remove extra carbs and fat, so you’re only getting the good stuff with every serving. The removal of these elements is geared toward bloat-free digestion.

Testers say it also tastes great, giving especially high marks to the French Vanilla flavor. “I really like the flavor of this one. It tastes like a vanilla creamer!” says Kayla Godfrey. “This is delicious. Great vanilla taste,” says Carlo Barajas.

You’ve probably seen that one of the biggest general complaints about protein powder is it can taste “chalky” and leave you with an off-putting aftertaste. Our testing team tried Gainful’s Caffe Mocha flavor, and liked the subtle, not-too-sweet flavor profile. “This reminds me of an at-home cappuccino mix,” says Barry Bridges. “The coffee flavor is very light—I’d say it’s more of a chocolate flavor,” adds Rachael Harris.

If you’re not a fan of coffee flavors, Gainful offers nine total flavors in individual-use packets, so you can pick and choose what you’re craving each day. Nastasi, who has tried many different Gainful Protein Powder flavors, says the Chocolate Peanut Butter, Caffe Mocha, and Sea Salt Caramel are his favorites.

Whey protein is a concentrated protein source derived from cow’s milk, which contains two major proteins called casein and whey (4). Whey accounts for 20 percent of milk protein, and is considered a high-quality protein source. Cow’s milk protein is considered a complete protein because it contains all nine essential amino acids required by the body (5).

Beyond basic nutrition, whey protein (6) may offer specific health benefits, such as enhanced immune function (7) and cardiometabolic health (8). Usually, whey is sold in powder form, which can be blended with water or other liquids or added to soft foods. Also, people use whey protein powder in cooking, which adds nutritional value to baked goods. Food manufacturers use whey formulations rather than cream, butter, or egg ingredients to make high-protein, low-fat products.

When you browse online or at your local nutrition shop for whey protein products, you’ll probably notice different forms of whey. The main difference in the types of whey protein is how they’re processed. The three most common forms of whey protein are concentrate, isolate, and hydrolysate (hydrolyzed whey).

Whey protein concentrate (WPC) is the least processed form of whey, so it contains the highest levels of lactose (milk sugar), fat, carbohydrates, and nutrients. Food manufacturers use WPC (9) to replace fresh dairy and eggs in products like sauces, soups, and baked goods because it adds flavor, color, and texture and extends shelf-life (10). However, it has the lowest protein content out of the three—typically 70 to 80 percent.

Whey protein isolate (WPI) is made when whey is filtered and processed. It contains the most protein, 90 percent or more, and less lactose. Because of its higher protein content, sports nutrition companies often prefer WPI for use in supplements, protein bars, and other protein products (11). However, it lacks some of the beneficial nutrients found in the concentrated form (12).

Whey protein hydrolysate (WPH), also known as hydrolyzed whey, is produced by a process called partial hydrolysis, which breaks down whey protein for easier absorption (13). WPH is digested faster than WPC or WPI (14), so it causes a 28 to 43 percent increase in blood sugar levels (15). Diabetics don’t have to worry about this, though. Protein digestion is slow. In fact, recent research suggests that whey protein improves glycemic (blood sugar) control (16).

The real benefit of a whey protein powder is that it’s an incredibly convenient and high-quality source of dietary protein. However, if you consume enough dietary protein through meat, dairy, legumes, and other foods, then you don’t need a protein powder to achieve your health and fitness goals. However, if you’re having trouble consuming enough protein through your diet alone, then adding a protein powder to your daily routine can have some real benefits.

Whey protein is rich in essential amino acids, including BCAAs, which can be beneficial for supporting muscle integrity and growth with training (17). Adding a protein powder for muscle gain to your daily diet can be a great way to help maximize your dietary protein intake and stimulate muscle growth.

When you’re in a caloric deficit with the goal of losing weight, you want to ensure that the weight you’re losing is primarily fat and not muscle. Eating a diet rich in protein helps preserve the lean muscle mass you’ve worked hard to achieve and enables your body to prioritize burning fat for energy.

Consuming whey protein has a satiating effect, meaning that it helps you feel full for a longer period of time. High protein diets help with weight loss by regulating your hunger levels and therefore reducing the amount of total calories you consume throughout the day.

In order to properly use a whey protein powder, you should first determine how much protein you should be eating on a daily basis. The amount of protein you consume is dependent on your fitness goals and current body weight, activity level, and physique. A simple way to calculate your daily protein intake is by multiplying your body weight by 0.8. The resulting number is how many grams of protein you should consume each day. This should provide most active individuals with sufficient protein intake. Remember that whey protein powder is a supplement and shouldn’t be your main source of dietary protein.

As far as how to consume this protein powder, you should follow the instructions on the supplement label. This usually entails mixing one scoop of protein powder with 10 to 12 ounces of your favorite beverage. It can also be mixed in a smoothie or foods like oatmeal and pancake batter. Whey protein powder can be consumed at any time of the day, but it’s usually utilized as a post-workout supplement to begin repairing muscle tissue.

When used in moderation, protein powder is free of side effects and generally considered safe for healthy adults. However, consuming large amounts of protein powder can lead to digestive issues, dehydration, and (potentially) nutrient deficiencies. It’s important to use whey protein powder as part of a balanced diet and not as your main source of dietary protein. If you experience any unusual symptoms after using protein powder, stop use immediately and consult a healthcare professional.

A whey protein powder will benefit anyone who is looking to increase their daily protein consumption and has trouble doing so through their diet alone. This is especially relevant for very active individuals, such as athletes, bodybuilders, and fitness enthusiasts who have increased protein demands due to their workouts and training.

Another segment of the population that may benefit from using a whey protein powder is older adults. As we age, our bodies become less efficient at absorbing protein from food (18). Using protein supplements can be an easy way for older adults to meet their daily protein needs and support muscle health.

When picking a whey protein product, there are a few factors to consider, including the type of protein, taste, nutrition, additives/allergies, and price.

Check the ingredients list to see what type of whey the protein powder contains. Some brands will use a blend of whey forms.

Whey proteins come in a wide variety of flavors. You’ll find options from unflavored to vanilla, chocolate orange, and summer berries, to name a few. Taste is important because you want a protein supplement you’ll enjoy. When just starting to supplement your protein intake, try a small container or buy samples of flavors you might enjoy and get creative with your add-ins. You can try fruits, flavored milks, or juices to create new flavors that fit your taste preference.

Check the whey protein label for the amount of protein per serving, and factor it into your daily protein intake. Most protein powders have around 25 grams per serving, which is an ideal dosage to maximize muscle protein synthesis (19). Also look for calories, fats, carbs, fiber, vitamins, and minerals and even amino acid profiles. Make sure that the supplement you choose gives you the maximum benefit without unnecessary add-ins.

Read the ingredients section, too. Look for additives or allergens that you want or need to avoid. For example, labels warn you if the whey powder contains soy or was processed in a facility with nuts.

The protein powders on our list give you a good idea of the price range for whey supplements. Our top picks vary from $1.16 to $3.41 per serving or $34 to $95 per container, so there’s an option for most budgets.

It depends on your body’s unique needs and health and fitness goals. You should include protein with meals or snacks every three to five hours (20), but no one should rely solely on protein powder because that would eliminate other nutritious whole foods from the diet.One whey protein drink per day is reasonable. Check with your doctor if you want to use whey protein to replace more than one meal.

Yes, whey protein powder is generally considered safe for healthy individuals when used in moderation. If you have any pre-existing medical conditions or have a severe lactose intolerance, consult with a healthcare professional before adding a whey protein powder to your diet.

There really is no “best time” to take a whey protein powder supplement. Instead, your timing depends on your individual goals and lifestyle. Some people enjoy a protein shake in the morning as a quick and easy breakfast option they can have on the go, while others prefer to consume it immediately after a workout to support muscle growth and recovery.Just remember that whey protein powder should be used as a supplement to a well-balanced diet, and should not be used as a replacement for whole nutrient-dense foods. The timing of when you consume the whey protein is less important than your overall protein intake throughout the day.

From keeping you satiated to helping you improve your performance in the gym, whey protein powder can certainly help you lose weight. Research has even shown that whey protein may reduce abdominal fat when combined with weight training (21).

If overused, whey protein can cause side effects (22), including kidney or liver damage, aggression, acne, and a disruption in gut bacteria. Since most people don’t consume more than one serving of whey protein per day, overconsumption is rare and takes time to develop. If you would like to add an extra layer of protection for your gut bacteria, you can even take a high-quality prebiotic or ensure you consume a variety of fruits and vegetables on a regular basis.

The best way to know if your whey protein is high quality is to read the labels. Check out the whey source, nutritional profile, and ingredient list. Quality wheys use traceable, organic, and certified ingredients. Also, high-quality whey products avoid fillers and artificial sweeteners. Another sign that you have a good quality whey is when the labels include certifications and seals from third-party approvals. These show that the manufacturer has proven the quality by established standards.

Promo Rewards typically drop in the first week of each month. Set a recurring reminder to check the FlyingBlue.com Promo Rewards page. Consistency is the single biggest factor in landing these deals.

Maintain balances in Chase UR, Amex MR, Citi ThankYou, or Capital One. When a promo appears, you need to transfer and book quickly. Having points spread across programs gives you flexibility and instant transfer capability.

When the monthly promo drops, scan the route list for your target destinations. If your preferred city is not on promotion, check connecting cities. A promo flight to Paris or Amsterdam plus a cheap intra-Europe connection can still deliver outstanding value.

Once you find availability at the promo price, transfer points from your preferred credit card program. Chase and Amex transfers to Flying Blue are typically instant. Complete the booking on FlyingBlue.com before availability disappears.

Before finalizing, check the total out-of-pocket cost including taxes and surcharges. Air France and KLM do charge fuel surcharges on award tickets ($200-$400). Factor this into your value calculation to ensure the redemption still makes financial sense versus a paid fare.

Picture this: you settle into a fully flat bed at 35,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, the city lights of New York fading behind you. In seven hours, you'll be in Paris. But right now, in this seat — a seat that costs upward of $6,000 in cash — you paid 53,000 points to be here. That's the Air France Business Class experience on the JFK–CDG route, and it's one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions available to the ChooseFI community today. Let's talk about the math, because the math is what makes this a genuine FI moment. A round-trip business class ticket between New York and Paris on Air France routinely retails for $3,000 on the low end and climbs to $6,000 or beyond during peak travel periods. At 53,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, you're looking at a value of **5.7 to 11.3 cents per point** — in a world where most points are considered excellent at 1.5 to 2 cents. You are, quite literally, squeezing 3 to 7 times the average value out of every mile you've earned. The pricing inefficiency here is real and it's structural. Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program releases discounted award seats monthly, sometimes cutting standard pricing by 25–50%. When a Promo Reward surfaces on a transatlantic business class route, the gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you pay in miles becomes almost absurd. A $4,000 cash ticket redeemable for 53,000 points you transferred at no cost from your Chase Sapphire Reserve? That's **7.5 cents per point** — money that your future self will thank you for. Beyond the numbers is the *experience* itself. Air France's long-haul business class product on the Boeing 777-300ER features a fully flat bed in a 1-2-1 configuration, direct aisle access from every seat, genuine French hospitality, and a meal service that feels like a restaurant, not an afterthought. This isn't a product you suffer through — it's one you savor. For a community that builds wealth intentionally so they can live fully, this is exactly what travel rewards are designed to unlock: a world-class experience at a fraction of the cost, because you understood the system.

Monthly promotional pricing makes premium European travel consistently accessible

The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

This is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

The transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear quickly.

One nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

Finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. The booking window opens 359 days in advance — plan accordingly.

Head to FlyingBlue.com at the beginning of each month — Promo Rewards are typically released in the first week. Navigate to the "Promo Rewards" section under the Awards tab. You're looking for transatlantic routes in business class (referred to as "Business" or "La Première" on the site). Bookmark the page and set a calendar reminder. You can also follow ChooseFI community forums, frequent flyer blogs, and Flying Blue's social accounts, which announce Promo Rewards as they drop. When a JFK–CDG or similar North America–Europe business class Promo Reward appears at 53,000 miles, you're in the window.

Once you've identified a Promo Reward route, search for availability directly on FlyingBlue.com. Use the award search tool, select "Business" class, and enter your travel dates. Promo Reward seats are labeled distinctly in the results. If you see them, note the exact flight numbers, dates, and total miles required before doing anything else. Don't transfer points yet — just confirm the seats exist and are bookable.

Determine which transferable currency you'll use. If you have Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, those are your fastest options — transfers to Flying Blue are instant. Log into your credit card portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards or americanexpress.com/rewards) and confirm you have at least 53,000 points available per person traveling in business class.

Initiate the transfer from your credit card rewards portal. Enter your Flying Blue membership number exactly as it appears on your account. For Chase and Amex, transfers post instantly — refresh your Flying Blue account and the miles should appear within minutes. For Capital One or Bilt, allow 1–2 days. For Marriott Bonvoy, note the 3:1 ratio (you'll need 159,000 Bonvoy points for 53,000 Flying Blue miles) and allow 1–5 days.

Return to FlyingBlue.com, log in with your miles now posted, and complete the award booking. Select the Promo Reward fare, confirm the passenger details, and review the fee breakdown carefully — verify that surcharges are eliminated or minimal. Pay the government taxes (typically $50–$150 transatlantic) with a credit card.

If Promo Reward seats aren't available on your dates, don't give up. Check standard award availability on Flying Blue — the pricing will be higher, but the experience is identical. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

Unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

Do this: Set a recurring monthly calendar reminder for Promo Rewards. Promo Rewards drop in the first week of each month and popular routes sell out fast. The readers who consistently land these redemptions aren't lucky — they're systematic. Mark the first Monday of every month as your "check Flying Blue" day.

Do this: Use an open-jaw routing to maximize your Europe trip. Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into one city and out of another within a single award booking. Fly JFK → CDG, travel through France, and fly home from AMS → JFK. You've just built a multi-city trip without paying for positioning flights — and used a single 53,000-mile award to do it.

Do this: Transfer points only after confirming availability. This cannot be overstated. Transfers from Chase and Amex are instant, but they are also irreversible. Never initiate a transfer until you have confirmed, with your own eyes, that the award seat is available and bookable. The five-minute shortcut of transferring first has stranded miles in countless accounts.

Avoid this: Booking standard dynamic awards without checking Promo Rewards first. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing on standard awards can be significantly higher than Promo Reward pricing — sometimes 30–50% more miles for the exact same seat. Always check if the month's Promo Rewards include your route before defaulting to a standard award.

Avoid this: Ignoring the surcharge line item. On standard (non-Promo) Flying Blue awards for Air France flights, carrier surcharges can add $200–$500 to your out-of-pocket cost. This doesn't eliminate the value, but it changes the math. Always review the full fee breakdown before confirming. Promo Rewards typically waive these surcharges — another reason to prioritize them.

Do this: Stack earning across multiple cards. You don't need to earn 53,000 points on a single card. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to Flying Blue at 1:1. Accumulate across programs, then choose the best transfer source when a Promo Reward surfaces. This flexibility is a structural advantage of the ChooseFI approach to travel rewards.

Know your expiry window. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one transaction (even a small earning or redemption) every two years to protect your balance.

This redemption is built for the intentional traveler — someone who has spent time accumulating points on one or more major transferable currencies and is ready to deploy them strategically rather than cash them in for coffee and Amazon gift cards.

Minimum requirements: You'll want at least 53,000 points in a single transferable currency (Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, or Bilt) or the ability to combine balances to reach that threshold. No Flying Blue status is required — this is available to any member.

For popular summer routes, start checking Promo Rewards at month-eight to month-ten before your trip. - **Follow community resources.** The ChooseFI community and frequent flyer forums will alert you when a strong Promo Reward drops — you don't have to monitor alone. - **Practice the search before you need it.** Log into FlyingBlue.com today and run a practice award search. Get comfortable with the interface before you're racing to book a Promo Reward seat. If you can earn miles and check a website once a month, you can execute this redemption. Major US-to-Europe routes like JFK-CDG or JFK-AMS tend to appear on the Promo Rewards list every 2-4 months. Less popular routes may appear less frequently. The key is consistent monthly monitoring so you catch the promotion when it appears for your target destination.

Flying Blue does not offer formal stopover benefits on award tickets. However, you can book a one-way promo award to your gateway city and then add a separate low-cost carrier or train connection to your final destination. Many travelers use this strategy to explore Paris or Amsterdam for a few days before continuing onward.

Yes. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Any qualifying activity resets the clock, including earning miles through a flight, credit card transaction, or transfer partner. A single small transfer from Chase or Amex every two years is sufficient to keep your miles alive.

Both airlines offer lie-flat business class seats with direct aisle access on long-haul aircraft. Air France's cabin tends to emphasize French culinary presentation and wine service, while KLM has a more understated Dutch design aesthetic. Both are solid products. When booking through Flying Blue, you can choose either airline based on routing, schedule, or cabin preference.

Flying Blue Promo Rewards turn business class to Europe from a special-occasion splurge into a repeatable system. By monitoring monthly promotions, maintaining transfer-ready points across multiple programs, and booking when your route appears at a discount, you can consistently fly lie-flat to European destinations for 50,000-62,000 miles. #8753. The Best Compact Rowing Machines for Small Spaces in 2025

A smaller footprint doesn’t mean you have to miss out. Here are the best compact rowing machines for a top-notch workout.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

If you’re limited on space, don’t let the length of a rowing machine deter you. While there are many great rowing machines on the market, there are also some awesome compact alternatives that offer all the same tech features you’ll find in other cardio machines.

During our search for the best compact rowing machine, we found an array of excellent standalone options and options that fit in well with other top-rated home gym equipment. We considered the overall footprint and other key features, and scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each product. Below is our list of the best compact home rowing machines available.

The rowing machines included in this list were carefully selected based on what most users would want out of a rowing machine, keeping in mind that they needed to have a smaller footprint and folding or upright storage options. We evaluated each choice based on size, portability, cost, high-tech features, versatility, and durability. We also scoured the reviews to see what users had to say about each rowing machine.

On the Hydrow website, the Hydrow Wave is rated 4.6/5 stars with over 9,000 reviews at the time of writing. It’s the brand’s compact, budget-friendly option for those who want to elevate their at-home workout routine. The length is just 80 inches, which is the shortest on this list, and the overall size is 30 percent shorter than the original Hydrow Rower. You cannot fold it, but there is the option to store it upright using The Hydrow Wave Vertical Anchor. This is a wall-mounted strap that holds the rower upright. It costs an additional $190, which is a bit on the pricey side.

The frame is made of aluminum and steel. It has a flat anthracite polymer body, which is a durable and lightweight material. The handle has an ergonomic design for a low-stress grip, and the strap is made from water- and rot-resistant polyester webbing. It also has a patented electromagnetic drag system that mimics the experience of rowing on open water.

Overall, the reviews on the Hydrow website are positive, and many mention how quiet the machine is and how much they like the small footprint. One review says, “The machine is such great quality. It’s quiet and sleek looking.” The critical reviews make up 3 percent of the overall reviews and state issues like non-working parts being delivered. However, Hydrow has responded to each review to resolve any issues.

The NordicTrack RW700 has a 10-inch HD touchscreen you can tilt and pivot to follow along with an iFIT workout led by your favorite trainer on or off the rower. An iFIT subscription is $39 per month, and you’ll have access to live and on-demand classes. Membership to the fitness app is not required to use the rower; however, you won’t have access to trainer-led classes without it.

A trainer-led rowing workout gives you the option to row on the open water for a more scenic experience, and there are also studio sessions. The resistance is adjusted automatically among 26 resistance levels during each class, so you don’t need to worry about stopping to make changes. The oversized foot pedals have adjustable nylon foot straps with quick release, which is excellent for those who want to incorporate movements off the rower into their workout.

The rail is 87 inches long and made from durable steel. It has an inertia-enhanced flywheel, so it should maintain a smooth rotation. If you have a shared space, the NordicTrack RW700 rower has a magnetic resistance system that creates tension against the flywheel without touching, making it a quieter option. After your workout, this magnetic rowing machine can be moved using the front wheels, but it can’t be folded.

The flywheel has been designed to maintain inertia and rotate smoothly, and the steel rail is oversized to help keep you stable. The large, pivoting foot pedals with adjustable nylon straps keep your feet in place, and the seat is molded with comfort in mind.

If you like to incorporate other movements into your rowing workout or train off of the rower, the Echelon Row-s has a 22-inch HD touchscreen that can be flipped 180 degrees. While an Echelon Fit subscription is not required, the extra $35/month workout app gives you access to over 40 live classes and more than 1,000 on-demand workouts from its library, including rowing, biking, running, and functional training classes.

The ergonomic design of the seat and the ability to adjust the foot platforms to a comfortable position help you maintain proper posture and alignment. If you’re short on space, the length goes from 84 inches long to just 41 inches long when folded. On the Echelon website, this rower is rated 4.6/5 stars. “The machine looks great, operates very quietly, and gives a great workout no matter your level,” says reviewer Brett P.

Dimensions: 87.02" L x 22.0" W x 47.24" H

Storage: Folds in half for vertical storage

Available programming: Live and on-demand workouts, scenic rows

The NordicTrack RW600 balances great tech features and an accessible price, making it a great value. The 10-inch screen is an excellent option for those who want to take instructor-led classes using an iFIT membership. NordicTrack’s patented Silent Magnetic Resistance can be adjusted up to 26 levels automatically in an iFIT class or manually as needed.

The pivoting foot pedals are oversized, and the nylon straps keep your feet secure. The handlebar has a soft grip, and the molded seat is designed to help you feel comfortable. When your workout is finished, the NordicTrack RW600 can be folded and stored out of the way.

What factors should you consider before you pull the trigger on a rower? Here’s what we’d recommend you take into account as you ponder your purchase decision:

Once you’ve decided on your rower location, it’s a good idea to measure the length, width, and height of your space to determine what size machine works best. You’ll want to measure height to see if you have enough clearance for rowers to be stored upright.

After measuring, think about how much you’re willing to spend. Take into consideration any additional costs such as a monthly subscription. Some rowers also have add-ons for purchase, such as a lumbar support system or seat upgrade.

Ask yourself: How many levels of resistance do I need? Am I looking for an HD touchscreen with trainer-led classes or do I prefer a more simplistic display? Other features such as a magnetic resistance system may be important if you’re in a shared space and need a quieter machine. The rower’s maximum height and/or weight capacity may also play a role in your decision as well.

Rowing allows you to implement low-impact, cardio-based training, and you can adjust the resistance for a strength-focused session. It’s a full-body workout that uses 86 percent of your muscles. With each stroke, you’re using your core and legs for the initial pull and finishing the rowing movement by using your upper body. Since you’re in a seated position, there’s less pressure on your knee and ankle joints.

Getting all four types of exercise (endurance, strength, balance, and flexibility) has benefits, according to The National Institute of Health (NIH). A rowing machine can be utilized for two types: endurance and strength. Many rowing machines have built-in programs or subscriptions that offer classes geared toward building strength and endurance.

Rowing is a great way to build strength and endurance while working various muscle groups. There are choices to suit a variety of budgets with different storage options and sizes. Figuring out how much space you have, your price range and the features you’d like will help you choose the best compact rowing machine for you.

The machines on this list range from just over $700 to around $2,000. You can find a rower in your price range, but if you opt for a rower under, say, $200, you may be compromising quality.

Typically, rowing machine length ranges between six to nine feet with more compact options at six or seven feet long.

The level of resistance that’s best for you depends on your fitness level, experience, and goals. Overall, you don’t want your workout to be too easy or so challenging you don’t accomplish the goal of your training session.

Compact rowing machines usually have air or magnetic resistance, and some options implement both.
